>From: "Wes Thomas" <west@sonic.net>

>rick stanton [mailto:arider2@hotmail.com] said:
>
> >better understanding of the technical aspects.I'm probably going to be a
> >hard advocate in favor of my "external" noise/hearing viewpoint
>
>Rick, could you explain what that viewpoint is? Are you saying you are
>hearing sounds directly? How would the RF from NLK get converted into sound
>externally? I don't know of any mechanism for that, but if there were by
>some unknown process, and if you're hearing them, why are they not audible
>to other people? Do you have more acute hearing in the low-frequency range?
>
> >They still emminate from every direction, thats part of
> >why I still believe they are external. I cant seem to caulk my ear and 
>tell
> >which direction the tones are coming from.
>
>Right, that's characteristic of low-frequency sound perception. You can
>confirm that by connecting only a subwoofer speaker to your stereo, closing
>your eyes, then trying to determine the speaker location. You'll find it's
>difficult to localize unless you sense pressure waves directly with your
>body. At higher frequencies, the geometry of the ears and the phase
>difference (time delay) of sound reaching the two ears, along with 
>frequency
>attentation differences (high frequencies will be reduced in one ear if 
>they
>originate on the opposite side of the head), along with room reflections,
>all provide cues that the human acoustic system uses at higher frequencies
>to localize sound. That's why you can focus on one conversation in a 
>crowded
>room (the "cocktail party effect"). So it's reasonable (I don't have a
>reference to support this, so consider it informed speculation) to assume
>that thermoelastic-generating sound (converted from RF) within the skull
>would sound identical to sound originating from outside, since outside 
>sound
>lacks localization cues, especially that portion that travels to the 
>cochlea
>via bone conduction in the head (bone conduction is higher at lower
>frequencies), where there are no localization cues from the outer ear.
>Bottom line: the sounds you hear are most likely endogenous (generated
>inside your head, either by RF, some anomaly in your acoustic system
>creating artifacts, or some other process). Another possibility is that you
>are hearing exogenous (externally generated) sounds generated by some other
>process (not RF).
>
>I hope all that makes sense? Scott may want to review that for accuracy.
>
> >was actually feeling the broadcast!!! The surface of my skin felt 
>slightly
> >tingly, like the hairs standing up, I looked at my arms and the hairs 
>were
> >not extended
>
>There are at least two possibilities here:
>
>1. You were sensing a high-voltage 60 Hz power line. Humans perceive 60 Hz
>electric fields greater than approximately 15 kV/m (kilovolts per meter) as
>"tingling" caused by vibration of hairs [1, p. 355]. (Note: the safety 
>limit
>for exposure to electric fields from high-voltage power lines is 4 to 10
>kV/m [1, p. 466], depending on which standard, so you were risking shock
>from induced current and should avoid that area.) This is the most likely
>explanation. How far from high voltage power lines in the area were you
>standing? These high-voltage lines would be required to provide the power 
>to
>drive the high-power 192 kW NLK transmitter.
>
>2. You were sensing the 24 kHz signal directly. I don't know of any 
>research
>regarding sensing frequencies in that range with body hairs, so my best
>speculation is that explanation #1 above is more likely. I'd like to be
>proved wrong on this.
>
> >but the force was penetrating my body, definitely bombarding it
> > as if I were in a strong magnetic field.
>
>Could you be more specific about what your sensations were? The only
>mechanism
>we have for sensing magnetic fields is visual phosphenes (the "stars in 
>your
>eyes" visual effect you get when you rub your eyes vigorously or get hit in
>the head), caused by magnetic stimulation of the retina [1, p. 387], so
>unless you saw "stars" that's not likely.
>
>References:
>
>[1] Reilly, Patrick J., Applied Bioelectricity, Springer-Verlag, 1998
>

Hello,

Something in Spiritwalker's recent post reminded me of some of 
the tenets of the Hopi religion.  (Well, a number of things, but this 
one I found particularly interesting).  Remember he spoke of whole 
planets as tuning forks, of resonances on a universal scale?  This 
is very ancient knowledge.  The Hopi elaborate:  they say that the 
twins who live at the north and south poles of the Earth's axis send 
out resonances--hums--that people "with the doors in the top of 
their heads open" (that is, people who are open to wisdom and are 
listening), can hear.  In fact, people are meant to hear these tones. 
  
What I find interesting is this:  we talk of only hearing the hum in 
recent years, yet here are a people who have been hearing hums 
for many hundreds--even thousands--of years.  Enough so that they 
worked it into their religion.

I'd just like to point out that when you are sincerely searching for 
the truth, everyone has something of some interest to contribute.  
Keep those doors on the tops of your head open...

Cristi

> I do not, nor have I ever felt, "pressure" on my body or pressure in my

More valuable tips, thanks Rick. This implies that Carolyn and Anne are
perceiving infrasonic waves (sounds under 20 Hz) while you are not.
Infrasonics are generated by large fans, refrigerators, idling trucks,
electricity generators, and other devices. While they are not audible, there
may be concomitant audible frequencies also generated by the same device
that are audible as low frequency pulsed sounds.

> ears all the time, under all conditions.But since I do not feel
> any pressure
> in my head, why would this same source (presumably)have a
> different affect
> on others responding here,than it does with me?

Rick, I don't understand that. Please rephrase? I wasn't aware that anyone
else was reporting any effects specifically from NLK. How would someone know
the source of a particular effect? It's more likely that there are a
plurality of sources of the diverse phenomena being reported on this list.

> why is it,
> that I hear 2 seperate tones? One would expect the stimuli to cause a
> certain,singular defined , reproducable type of tone or noise, to be
> detected by the ear. How can 2 seperate types of results(hearing
> tones) be
> present within the same 1 source (the hum)at the same time?

NLK operates at one RF frequency, but that frequency is frequency modulated.
You would not be hearing the single RF frequency (24.8 kHz is in the
ultrasonic range); you would be hearing the modulation frequencies on that
carrier frequency, just like when you listen to the radio, you're hearing
the multiple modulated audio signals, not the one RF signal.

NLK is designed to communicate with ships and submarines in the Pacific
Ocean, using cryptographically encoded pulses (similar to Morse code). It
transmits at 200 baud (approx. 200 bits per second), using a 50 Hz shift in
frequency for mark and space (binary on and off) coding
(http://db0sif.ernaehrung.uni-giessen.de/cgi-bin/dpcmd?R%20VLF%2017).
This means it actually transmits at two frequencies -- 24.850 kHz and 24.750
kHz -- and these frequencies are switched back and forth 200 times per
second. So there are two modulation components: 200 Hz and 50 Hz. Are these
the tones you're hearing? Note: 200 Hz is between G and G sharp just below
middle C on the piano. 50 Hz is slightly lower than standard 60 Hz hum.

> I dont believe
> our ear tissue and construction, would allow itself to react and vibrate
> efficiantly yet produce the 2 tones independantly.

The cochlea hairs vibrate simultaneously at many frequencies. That's why we
can listen to polyphonic music.

> which is heating up my inner ear,why wouldnt it also confuse the other
> normal hearing processes within my head?

Since our hearing evolved prior to modern pulsed RF, we would likely have no
mechanism to differentiate endogenous RF and normal (exogenous) sources.
This is implied by Frey's research.

> to be heating my inner ear

No, it's heating the brain, which expands thermoelastically and sends
pressure waves to the cochlea.

> doesnt everyone within the range feel or hear the same thing??!!

Ah, that's the big question. One guess: you are electrosensitive (2 percent
of the population is). See http://www.feb.se/FEB/AboutES.html. The hummers
I've interviewed at also electrosensitive. I'm curious if list members also
are. Please check your symptoms against this URL.

> travel on to see these towers, is also a road wich many people live on,
> these Towers are right in their own backyards

People may have adapted to the signals (the nervous system is able to adapt
and thus filter out some high-power RF signals, as Arthur Firstenberg
reported in his "No Place To Hide" newsletter April 2001).

> static electricity upon my entire body, no other outside affects that I
> could tell.. simply this massive pressure force surrounding me.

That implies a combination of an electric field and infrasonic generator.

Also, I just found the Hum map on the TaosHum site
(http://www.eskimo.com/~billb/hum/hum.html):
http://www.eskimo.com/~billb/hum/hum_map.gif

These clusters appear to correspond generally to Loran-C transmitter
locations at http://www.uscg.mil/hq/lsu/webpage/images/Loran-C_map.jpg.
Perhaps someone with a good statistics background can analyze this data to
come up with a more precise measure of correlation?

BTW, it would help if list reports used the "Hum" rating scale at
http://www.eskimo.com/~bilb/freenrg/humlev.txt

Conducting experiments with high voltage (40kv) STATIC audio in effort
to resonate/bounce echos off extraterrestrial objects since 1986, I must
support evidence that acoustic frequencies of intense static fields do
quite indeed cause a "tickling" sensation.  What becomes apparent upon
witness of such effect is that the tactile neurons are unable to respond
at frequencies greater than acoustic bass (around a few hundred hertz),
but yet there appear to be "bones" in the ear which can sense electrical
static/magnetic signals to beyond 100Khz.  I limit the top frequency
of experiments to 3Khz, but I have in past years been in the proximity
of certain surveilance equipment said to be operating at nearly .5 Mhz
and clearly (almost deafeningly) audible... it is of course possible,
however, that several high frequency components might conduct into a
resonant ortho-cavity with non-linear electrical character and yield
a beat frequency component..

S. Klabis / <http://www.scn.org/~sak/> in Phoenix Arizona, USA.

tones(each a little higher than the other).  The second set of sounds are 
actually frequencies.  It's like a high pitched whine or frequency(even

had to describe the sound, I would liken it to what electricity or a tens 
unit would sound like if we could hear its activity.  The frequencies even 
have different sounds.  When someone else was able to hear the sound, they 
liken it to "using a cell phone while passing through a canopy of trees".

Hi Raymond,

sorry I didn't have time to follow the links you suggested but will try
them later.

In my experiments with electret microphones I covered the infrasound
spectrum (<20 Hz) pretty well down to about 3 Hz. To date I have found
no correlation to my hum which is around 70 Hz.

In order to produce infrasound of fairly high amplitude, all one has to
do is cover mouth and nose and try to breath in and out (compress the
air volume trapped in the lungs) rapidly. This creates a sound wave of
several Hertz and if you do that behind a persons back, this person
won't hear anything despite the fact that the sound wave is of fairly
high amplitude (compared to other environmental sound waves in this
frequency region).

cheers, Peter.

hi fellow hummers,

for all in the vicinity of powerful military installations please consider this:
in order to generate the RF power, there have to be huge diesel powered
electricity generators. I doubt that the power comes out of the power mains
because this might be too unreliable for this kind of operation. As far as I
know from a similar installation here in Australia they run 4 huge diesel
powered generators which produce the necessary juice for pumping out a megawatt
of RF 24/7. And there is no doubt that these diesel engines produce their fair
share of acoustic noise which can probably be heard from 20...30 kilometres away
(rotational vibrations from the engine(s) might carry even farther). So there
may be an acoustic/vibrational component associated with any of these huge
transmitter sites.

cheers, Peter.

hi Doug and fellow hummers,

welcome to the list Doug.
Several months ago I downloaded a sine generator but forgot the link in the
meantime. Anyway, I have uploaded a copy of it so if you are interested give it
a go:
http://www.powerup.com.au/~pfreihof/hum/sinewave.zip (185 kByte)
http://www.powerup.com.au/~pfreihof/hum/sweepgen.exe (374 kByte)

the Sweepgen.exe is the unzipped version of the Sinewave.zip.

When using it, you shouldn't use the up and down arrows since these change the
frequency randomly and what's worse, the change in frequency won't get
displayed. Otherwise it is a great little program and it works really well on
my 166 MHz laptop.

I encourage everyone to use this program in connection with a set of reasonably
good quality ear(head)phones - walkman and discman ones are ok. Maybe this will
help to shed some light on the sometimes quite vague (sorry about this
expression) description of the hum pitch.
If you run this little program on a relatively quiet laptop (fan not running)
there is a method to determine one's hum pitch really accurately.

Now to your recordings using Spectrogram: It is hard to pinpoint the source for
your 10 Hz harmonics. Did you say these lines weaken during the weekend? If
yes, then this electrical noise most likely comes in via the power grid which
can get really polluted by industrial machinery.

Good luck with the sine generator, I look forward to reading about your
results.
cheers, Peter.

Hi, Franz

frosch wrote:
> 
> Dear Judy,
> when you moved from one area to another, how many days did it last until the hum
> reappeared?

In the beginning, when the hum was intermittent, I would not hear it
when I was away from home outside a 30 mile radius or so, and it would
be absent for as long as I was gone, whether it was a few hours or
several days.  There were also isolated areas close to home without hum
(like the parking lot at our library). Frequently it would be noticeable
again immediately on returning home, welcoming me as I stepped from my
car. In the beginning however, the hum would sometimes turn off for
days, weeks, or months at a time, so its presence or absence was
difficult to track in the context of returning home after being away.
Gradually, I started hearing hum in places which had previously been
silent, and since December, 1997 I have heard the hum at variable
intensity every place I have been except Salt Lake City.  So, for the
last four years, which were the years I have traveled a lot,
"reappearance" has not even been possible.

Hearing the hum 24/7 now has created problems in assessing other sounds
which may or may not be connected to the hum. Having no silent periods
for comparison, I can no longer determine whether new sounds I hear are
connected to the hum or not. It must be remembered however, that what I
call "hum" does not seem to be the sound most on this list call the
hum.  What you all are calling hum seems to be more like the second
sound I hear, which I call the rumble, an extremely low frequency
bumping tumbling sound which is similar to the hum recordings which I
have heard.  This sound has not changed much over the years.  It still
is intermittent; it is usually present during times of greatest hum
intensity, and I believe it may be acoustic, because when it is really
active it produces vibrations that can be felt, matching in pattern and
tempo the sound that I hear. To this day, I have only heard this second
component in a few places away from home: Oklahoma, New Mexico, and
Colorado

Sorry I can't be of more help. I don't think I ever experienced that
short time of silence after returning home that some others report. The
hum was usually waiting for me, or occasionally it seemed to be
temporarily off.

Best regards,

Judy

Try it on a laptop running from a battery if possible to eliminate external
power line noise (as Peter identified). Best guess: a motor that kicks in
periodically, either in your home or neighbor's. Run a .1 mf or larger
capacitor rated at 600 working volts from your AC into your audio in and run
the CoolEdit notch filter to remove 60/120 Hz to see if it's from your power
line (if you're not a qualified electronics tech, don't try this, it may
cause lethal shock).

One more suggestion here might be to run IBM Basic in "play"
or "sound" mode.. older versions of "A-basic" utilize the 
entire CPU rather than an externally dedicated generator to 
produce some fairly accurate musical tones... keep in mind
a digitally synthesized "sine-wave" will contain distortion
products equivalent to quantization error.. faster clocks
and higher resolution in successive approximation registers
help reduce this distortion... alternative #2 might be to
use an analog (tuned L/C or R/C) wave generator.. circuits
for these may be found in Popular Electronics magazines
dating back to the '60s.

>
>NLK operates at one RF frequency, but that frequency is frequency 
>modulated.
>You would not be hearing the single RF frequency (24.8 kHz is in the
>ultrasonic range); you would be hearing the modulation frequencies on that
>carrier frequency, just like when you listen to the radio, you're hearing
>the multiple modulated audio signals, not the one RF signal.
>
>NLK is designed to communicate with ships and submarines in the Pacific
>Ocean, using cryptographically encoded pulses (similar to Morse code). It
>transmits at 200 baud (approx. 200 bits per second), using a 50 Hz shift in
>frequency for mark and space (binary on and off) coding
>(http://db0sif.ernaehrung.uni-giessen.de/cgi-bin/dpcmd?R%20VLF%2017).
>This means it actually transmits at two frequencies -- 24.850 kHz and 
>24.750
>kHz -- and these frequencies are switched back and forth 200 times per
>second. So there are two modulation components: 200 Hz and 50 Hz. Are these
>the tones you're hearing? Note: 200 Hz is between G and G sharp just below
>middle C on the piano. 50 Hz is slightly lower than standard 60 Hz hum.
>
> > I dont believe
> > our ear tissue and construction, would allow itself to react and vibrate
> > efficiantly yet produce the 2 tones independantly.
>
>The cochlea hairs vibrate simultaneously at many frequencies. That's why we
>can listen to polyphonic music.
>
> > which is heating up my inner ear,why wouldnt it also confuse the other
> > normal hearing processes within my head?
>
>Since our hearing evolved prior to modern pulsed RF, we would likely have 
>no
>mechanism to differentiate endogenous RF and normal (exogenous) sources.
>This is implied by Frey's research.
>
> > to be heating my inner ear
>
>No, it's heating the brain, which expands thermoelastically and sends
>pressure waves to the cochlea.
>

>Conducting experiments with high voltage (40kv) STATIC audio in effort
>to resonate/bounce echos off extraterrestrial objects since 1986, I must
>support evidence that acoustic frequencies of intense static fields do
>quite indeed cause a "tickling" sensation.  What becomes apparent upon
>witness of such effect is that the tactile neurons are unable to respond
>at frequencies greater than acoustic bass (around a few hundred hertz),
>but yet there appear to be "bones" in the ear which can sense electrical
>static/magnetic signals to beyond 100Khz.  I limit the top frequency
>of experiments to 3Khz, but I have in past years been in the proximity
>of certain surveilance equipment said to be operating at nearly .5 Mhz
>and clearly (almost deafeningly) audible... it is of course possible,
>however, that several high frequency components might conduct into a
>resonant ortho-cavity with non-linear electrical character and yield
>a beat frequency component..
>
>S. Klabis / <http://www.scn.org/~sak/> in Phoenix Arizona, USA.
>

>
>In the beginning, when the hum was intermittent, I would not hear it
>when I was away from home outside a 30 mile radius or so, and it would
>be absent for as long as I was gone, whether it was a few hours or
>several days.  There were also isolated areas close to home without hum
>(like the parking lot at our library). Frequently it would be noticeable
>again immediately on returning home, welcoming me as I stepped from my
>car. In the beginning however, the hum would sometimes turn off for
>days, weeks, or months at a time, so its presence or absence was
>difficult to track in the context of returning home after being away.
>Gradually, I started hearing hum in places which had previously been
>silent, and since December, 1997 I have heard the hum at variable
>intensity every place I have been except Salt Lake City.  So, for the
>last four years, which were the years I have traveled a lot,
>"reappearance" has not even been possible.
>
>Hearing the hum 24/7 now has created problems in assessing other sounds
>which may or may not be connected to the hum. Having no silent periods
>for comparison, I can no longer determine whether new sounds I hear are
>connected to the hum or not. It must be remembered however, that what I
>call "hum" does not seem to be the sound most on this list call the
>hum.  What you all are calling hum seems to be more like the second
>sound I hear, which I call the rumble, an extremely low frequency
>bumping tumbling sound which is similar to the hum recordings which I
>have heard.  This sound has not changed much over the years.  It still
>is intermittent; it is usually present during times of greatest hum
>intensity, and I believe it may be acoustic, because when it is really
>active it produces vibrations that can be felt, matching in pattern and
>tempo the sound that I hear. To this day, I have only heard this second
>component in a few places away from home: Oklahoma, New Mexico, and
>Colorado
>

Dear Fellow Hummers,

        On characteristic of electro-magnetic waves is their ability to
travel along pre-existing wiring, transmitting any of what is going on at
the source.  I have often said "the hum" is apparent in my electrical
components.  It is in the audio buss of my stereo and VCR.  (This is easy
to understand as both radio and television transmissions are
electro-magnetic waves themselves)  It is pretty easy to interfear with
reception.  On the other hand, "the hum" causes our lights, both
flourescent and incandescent, to buzz.  On the phone line, there is a
ghostly echo, both products of low frequency electro-magnetic waves
propagating on existing signals, both wired and unwired.
        I have often speculated about the difference  between physiological
characteristics of low frequency electro-magnetic waves and low frequency
sound.  They have some similarities.  EM waves produce heat in the body as
tissue heats, not unlike gamma radiation at a low intensities.  The rest is
guess-work.  The brain operates in the 8-12 Hz range, and studies have done
that concluded the brain at first tries to ignore the external stimulus,
but eventually "locks on to" the outside signal.  This could be considered
mood or thought altering if it takes you from a beta to theta state or
vice-versa.  For me I know it effects my cognitive thought process.  If it
is sheer vibration in the air or electro-magnetic I don't know.  The
tingling some people feel could be either an electro-magnetic field, or
just vibration through sound waves.
        The easy way to decide would simply be to measure.  There is a
dedicated web page that outlines infrasound monitoring in machinery.  They
use a piezo-ceramic element with very low noise electronics.  I have read
accounts where microphones can document infrasound, as well as simple
frequency analysis in a sound program in a PC.  Then there are the
complicated arrays to measure infrasound resulting from global nuclear
explosions.  These are handled by the U.S. government.  With all this
technology, which is the most accurate?  Seems a simple compass would be
effected by low frequency electro-magnetic waves.  Vic Tandy is the UK
professor that has accurately measured infrasound in "haunted houses."

Cheers,

PR

Hi, Rick

rick stanton wrote:
> 
> Judy, is it possible you may be only hearing the lower tone? What I hear is
> always the two-tone sound, one a higher tone and the other is the lower
> tone(rumble,base, boom-box etc) 

I wouldn't really call what I hear a "tone". My sounds (all three of
them) contain multiple frequencies; components #1 (hum) and #3 (sizzle?)
are blended frequencies which all play together. The frequencies in #1
can interact with themselves to produce a beat.  Component #2 (rumble)
probably has the fewest frequencies but these are really hard to pick
out as they are all really in the cellar. The rumble is primarily a
bumping combustive type sound which really doesn't have any "tone" to
it. It contains the lowest frequencies I hear and I believe they are
just at the lower limit of hearing. I have always felt that there is
actually more sound involved with this than I can hear, and that I may
be hearing only the peaks of the highest frequencies, or the most
amplified portions of the sound. Component #1 (hum) is significantly
higher in frequency than component #2. #2 is definitely in the ELF range
maybe some of it might be ULF which I can't hear; #1 is probably VLF.
These two sound ranges do not play alternately as you have described.
Rather the rumble tumbles along intermittently within the hum. It's
presentation seems mostly irregular and random, although occasionally I
have noticed what seemed like brief patterns.  Sometimes when it is very
pronounced, it can assume a kind of "chugging" rotary quality and sounds
very mechanical.

Component #3 came along much later, by at least two years. It is a very
high frequency concoction of discordant frequencies that started out as
a brief sound which sounded like someone had scratched a wire on a
window, a sort of electric fish sound.  Over the years this component
has developed a greater duration when it plays, and now can last for
minutes to hours, is continuous and shimmering in quality, much like the
zinging of insects in trees, or the sound of a piece of electronic
equipment which has been turned on and makes a faint high-frequency
hum.  I have a stereo which duplicates the sound nearly exactly. It
drives me nuts.

I associate both component #2 and #3 with the original hum that I hear,
because I have never heard them play in the absence of the hum. They
also seem to occur when the accompanying hum is very intense. As I said
in my earlier post, I can't do this anyone, as now every sound I hear
has the hum in the background.

It doesn't seem that these sounds are similar to yours from your
description, and that is why I didn't write to you earlier. But for the
new people on the list I too have lived in a rural setting since 1976,
and the last 10 years have been in semi-wilderness, where there are no
man-made sounds at all, except an occasional plane overhead or a car
rattling along the unpaved road that comes down into our valley.  In the
beginning I could escape the hum by merely stepping outside. It would
recur immediately on re-entering the house.  In my opinion, this
phenomenon speaks against tinnitus or other pathological condition
causing the hum, as the house seems to amplify the hum, which would
suggest an external signal of some sort.  Now, however, I can hear the
hum outside as well. I thought for a long time that the hum might be
radio frequency, as it changes at times with the occurrence of solar
flares and geomag storming. However, most on this list felt that was not
a viable assumption. I also seem to live underneath a aircraft
training/testing corridor between Travis Air Force base and someplace in
Nevada, and have heard strange aircraft sounds from time to time, which
cannot be defined as anything I have experienced before. My home is
all-electric, and water pipes are made of PVC. Whether anything here is
helpful to anyone I haven't a clue, but there it is for what it's
worth...

Judy

I downloaded the sweepgen.exe file offered by a recent new contributor =
(and I've deleted that e-mail by mistake) so I don't have the link =
handy.  A sweetheart of a utility!  Anyway,  I have always suspected =
that the hum I hear is below 20 HZ,  and the sinewave generator =
confirmed that.  The hum was good and loud last evening,  and I tuned =
the sweep generator up and down and zeroed in on my hum at 17 HZ.  I =
would say that rather strongly implicates Loran-C as the hum source in =
my case at least.  As more people join this forum it is becoming clear =
that there is not one universal source,  but any number of them =
involving an unknown range of frequencies.  Now that the link between RF =
and auditory response (whether virtual or actual) has been fairly well =
established we can assume that there will be many frequencies and =
modulations within those frequencies that will cause a noticeable =
symptom in sensitive individuals.  The two recent posts describing a =
mosquito-like whine might be the result of microwaves.  A microwave =
carrier with a pulse modulation around 4,000HZ could very well sound =
like a mosquito to someone with the right "receive" characteristics,  =
whatever those may be.  I suggest everyone on this list that hasn't =
already confirmed the exact frequency of their particular hum should =
download "sweepgen.exe" and determine their pitch.  The software takes =
up very little space,  downloads in minutes,  and is very simple to use. =
 Knowing exactly,  rather than guessing the frequency,  could offer =
clues in many cases that will be vastly better than pure guesswork.

Now,  as to approaching a Loran-C transmitter to see if the hum gets =
louder,  I wonder if there is a point at which you enter into near-field =
effect and there could in fact be a complete stoppage of the hum at =
close proximity.  Wes,  you have a much better grasp of radio physics =
than most of us it seems so I am offering this just as a suggestion.  =
Also,  to explain the very curious symptoms Rick describes which are not =
at all typical,  I wonder if the two "tones" as well as the physical =
sensations could be explained by his being in near field effect.  I am =
much farther from any transmitter and only get the cyclic,  low rumble,  =
the "idling diesel". =20

What a shame that the respective Coast Guards made the decision to =
maintain the Loran-C system indefinitely.  Some of the world's most =
powerful transmitters broadcasting at or near human brain wave =
frequencies,  and for no good reason as the system is completely =
obsolete....it is sheer idiocy.  =20

An interesting point Paul Reichle made about the brain at first trying =
to ignore the signal,  but eventually giving in and locking on to it.  =
This could explain the curious delay that many,  including myself,  have =
experienced time after time,  when returning home after an absence,  =
being hum free for a period up to several days before it starts again.  =
It makes sense that having evolved without RF's in our environment we =
are not well equipped to resist this artificial intrusion.

larger overview and new ideas.  It seems as if we are getting somewhere =
at last.

From: Alf Bangert [mailto:alfbangert@telus.net]

> Zeroed in on my hum at 17 HZ.

Alf, either you have extended hearing (beyond the usual 20 Hz limit) or
you're hearing an artifact, perhaps the first harmonic of 17 Hz at 28 Hz.
Can you (or someone on the list) take a look at the sweepgen signal (at the
computer audio out) on a scope to see how accurate and harmonic-free it is?
There may be some dependence on computer clock speed or CPU loading,
depending on how the algorithm is written, as I think someone on the list
stated or implied. I don't have my scope set up at the moment. Be careful
that you don't overdrive the audio (excessive volume on the input or
output), which can generate spurious signals.

>I would say that rather strongly implicates Loran-C as the hum source in my
case at least.

For list members in England, check out the TETRA system, which broadcasts a
17.6 Hz modulated signal throughout the country. This may be a hum source
there. Biophysicist Dr. Gerard Hyland, University of Warwick, has written
what I think is the best analysis yet of the effects of RF on the brain:
THE PHYSIOLOGICAL AND ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS OF NON-IONISING ELECTROMAGNETIC
RADIATION, March 2001, a report to the European Parliament (working draft).
I've posted it to http:://www.sonic.net/~west/mc/hyland.htm.

"This Study focuses upon an aspect of how living organisms and humans in
particular can be adversely affected by highly coherent electromagnetic
fields of technological origin, in a way that is not entertained or
addressed by existing Safety Guidelines – namely, through the possibility of
non-thermal, frequency-specific influences of an informational nature."

Regarding TETRA, he says:

"A good example of the prevailing disregard for what might be termed
‘electromagnetic biocompatibility’ is the development of TETRA (Trans
European/or Terrestrial Enhanced Trunked Radio Access), which operates at
somewhat higher powers than does GSM, and over a much wider range of
microwave carrier frequencies.  Most disturbing, however, is the fact that
the basic frame repetition rate is here 17.6Hz.  For this frequency (which
lies in the range of beta brain-wave activity) is close both to that at
which a flashing visible light can provoke seizures in people with
photosensitive epilepsy4, and to the modulation frequency at which there is
a maximum in the expression of calcium ions from brain cells when they are
irradiated with amplitude modulated, low intensity RF radiation over a wide
range of carrier frequencies5-7; it should be remembered that these ions
play a crucial role in inter-cellular communication, any interference with
which could well undermine the integrity of the whole nervous system,
although the extent to which this actually occurs is, at present uncertain,
owing to a lack of the necessary research.  Furthermore, in consequence of
the lower frequency band assigned to the emergency services (380MHz -
400MHz), the penetration of the radiation is here much greater than it is
with GSM, facilitating its deeper access into the brain directly through the
skull."

>As more people join this forum it is becoming clear that
>there is not one universal source,  but any number
>of them involving an unknown range of frequencies.

This is an important point. There are liely many causes.

>Knowing exactly,  rather than guessing the frequency,
>could offer clues in many cases that will be vastly
>better than pure guesswork.

Agreed. More specifics in reports would be very helpful. Spell out time,
place, duration, conditions (weather, etc.), your environment (city,
apartment, remote house, near power lines, near airport, etc.). List members
should post an audiogram
(http://www.sfu.ca/sonic-studio/Audiogram.html) as a baseline for informed
discussion of their specific case.

>Now,  as to approaching a Loran-C transmitter
>to see if the hum gets louder,  I wonder if there
>is a point at which you enter into near-field effect
>and there could in fact be a complete stoppage
>of the hum at close proximity.

This is an excellent point. I alluded to Arthur Firstenberg's observation
that the human body adapts to higher levels of signals but not to lower
levels. We should look into this paradoxical effect.

>powerful transmitters broadcasting at or near human brain wave frequencies

See the Hyland report for more on that

>the brain at first trying to ignore the signal,
>but eventually giving in and locking on to it.

We need to explore that too. This might correspond to the exhaustion stage
in the "general adaption syndrome"?
http://www.bmb.psu.edu/courses/bisci004/gasyndrome.html. Also, different
degrees of entrainment (locking on) and other factors explain why some
people hear it and other do not:

"Since the physiological state of different people cannot, however, be
anticipated to be the same – depending as it does on factors such as the
stability of an individual’s brain rhythms against interference or
entrainment by the radiation, their already prevailing level of stress, and
the robustness of their immune system – it follows that identical exposure
to exactly the same radiation can entail quite different (non-thermal)
responses in different people (or even in the same person, depending on
his/her condition at the time of exposure88), quite unlike the case of
active electronic instruments."

This points the need to develop data on the general health level of persons
who report hum phenomena. Are they more prone to illness and exposed to
higher levels of stress? That would be consistent with Hyland's point.

First clue comes to mind here is ALL ELECTRIC / PVC.  PVC water
pipes are poor conductors of ground currents; worse PVC insulation
tends to rot and "leak" electrical current after 10-20 years... .
Strange noises due to said leakage/bad ground conditions might be
expected most especially in areas where wiring and/or electrical
ground connections intersect or meet vegitation or other organic
matter physically stimulated by said currents.

There is a type of "underground ROmex" (wire) on the market but
in my opinin it is unsuitable for long-term instalation MOST
especially in cases where a NEUTRAL return is expected.  THe
safest & QUIETEST underground wiring is FLOATED with a special
ISOLATION TRANSFORMER.  Running single-phase 117/220 with a 
neutral/ground introduces a chance of ground looping if the
path of least resistance for ground return exceeds that of
the neutral wiring (white wire).  A "floating" system will
eliminate the possibility of taking such a risk.

    S. Klabis / sak55@aztec.asu.edu / 602-252-1951

>I wouldn't really call what I hear a "tone". My sounds (all three of

>are blended frequencies which all play together. The frequencies in #1
>can interact with themselves to produce a beat.  Component #2 (rumble)
>probably has the fewest frequencies but these are really hard to pick
>out as they are all really in the cellar. The rumble is primarily a
>bumping combustive type sound which really doesn't have any "tone" to
>it. It contains the lowest frequencies I hear and I believe they are
>just at the lower limit of hearing. I have always felt that there is
>actually more sound involved with this than I can hear, and that I may
>be hearing only the peaks of the highest frequencies, or the most
>amplified portions of the sound. Component #1 (hum) is significantly
>higher in frequency than component #2. #2 is definitely in the ELF range
>maybe some of it might be ULF which I can't hear; #1 is probably VLF.
>These two sound ranges do not play alternately as you have described.
>Rather the rumble tumbles along intermittently within the hum. It's
>presentation seems mostly irregular and random, although occasionally I
>have noticed what seemed like brief patterns.  Sometimes when it is very
>pronounced, it can assume a kind of "chugging" rotary quality and sounds
>very mechanical.
>
>Component #3 came along much later, by at least two years. It is a very
>high frequency concoction of discordant frequencies that started out as
>a brief sound which sounded like someone had scratched a wire on a
>window, a sort of electric fish sound.  Over the years this component
>has developed a greater duration when it plays, and now can last for
>minutes to hours, is continuous and shimmering in quality, much like the
>zinging of insects in trees, or the sound of a piece of electronic
>equipment which has been turned on and makes a faint high-frequency
>hum.  I have a stereo which duplicates the sound nearly exactly. It
>drives me nuts.

>also seem to occur when the accompanying hum is very intense. As I said

>has the hum in the background.

Scott said:

> First clue comes to mind here is ALL ELECTRIC / PVC.  PVC water
> pipes are poor conductors of ground currents; worse PVC insulation
> tends to rot and "leak" electrical current after 10-20 years... .
> Strange noises due to said leakage/bad ground conditions

Do you have any references for the noises? Ground currents from incorrect
wiring have been shown to have surprising amounts of RF, 
even microwave, and can induce electrical hypersensitivity 
and various forms of illness. See:

http://www.indymedia.org/front.php3?article_id=42795
http://www.sncmfg.com/telecom/stray_voltage/dahlberg.html

It's also possible that audio tones could be a result of 
nonlinear rectification of modulated tones on random 
high-frequency ground currents. 

It would be a good research project to take a look at some of
these currents (in homes with hum problems) with an 
oscilloscope and see what floating around.

> >difference (time delay) of sound reaching the two ears, along with
> >frequency
> >attentation differences (high frequencies will be reduced in one ear if
> >they
> >originate on the opposite side of the head), along with room reflections,
> >all provide cues that the human acoustic system uses at higher
frequencies
> >to localize sound. That's why you can focus on one conversation in a
> >crowded
> >room (the "cocktail party effect"). So it's reasonable (I don't have a
> >reference to support this, so consider it informed speculation) to assume
> >that thermoelastic-generating sound (converted from RF) within the skull
> >would sound identical to sound originating from outside, since outside
> >sound
> >lacks localization cues, especially that portion that travels to the
> >cochlea
> >via bone conduction in the head (bone conduction is higher at lower
> >frequencies), where there are no localization cues from the outer ear.
> >Bottom line: the sounds you hear are most likely endogenous (generated
> >inside your head, either by RF, some anomaly in your acoustic system
> >creating artifacts, or some other process). Another possibility is that
you

other
> >process (not RF).

> NLK operates at one RF frequency, but that frequency is frequency
modulated.
> You would not be hearing the single RF frequency (24.8 kHz is in the
> ultrasonic range); you would be hearing the modulation frequencies on that
> carrier frequency, just like when you listen to the radio, you're hearing
> the multiple modulated audio signals, not the one RF signal.
>
> NLK is designed to communicate with ships and submarines in the Pacific
> Ocean, using cryptographically encoded pulses (similar to Morse code). It
> transmits at 200 baud (approx. 200 bits per second), using a 50 Hz shift
in
> frequency for mark and space (binary on and off) coding
> (http://db0sif.ernaehrung.uni-giessen.de/cgi-bin/dpcmd?R%20VLF%2017).
> This means it actually transmits at two frequencies -- 24.850 kHz and
24.750
> kHz -- and these frequencies are switched back and forth 200 times per
> second. So there are two modulation components: 200 Hz and 50 Hz. Are
these
> the tones you're hearing? Note: 200 Hz is between G and G sharp just below
> middle C on the piano. 50 Hz is slightly lower than standard 60 Hz hum.
>
> > I dont believe
> > our ear tissue and construction, would allow itself to react and vibrate
> > efficiantly yet produce the 2 tones independantly.
>
> The cochlea hairs vibrate simultaneously at many frequencies. That's why
we
> can listen to polyphonic music.

Yes: the key here to high frequency components is the NON-LINEAR 
device.  As a high current low frequency wave conducts through
such a semi-conducting device or oxidized connection a transient
signal is produced by said non-linear e/i characteristics.  As
an example, a standard silicone diode conducts in one direction
at a threshold of about .7 volts.  If a low frequency source is 
capable of producing a voltage greater than this, the resultant
angle of the vector into said conduction represents a smaller
period in time than would occur in a pure sinusoid.

Regarding biological sensititvity, I would guess the synaptic
terminals of a neuron might function in ways like a diode, but
my primary concern lies in an entirely different sphere yielding
to theory that magnetic fields (perpendicular to static fields)
physically agitate iron oxide in hemoglobin... have yet to see
much of anything published to this effect but thanks the same
for references..

> > > > >They still emminate from every direction, thats part of
> > > > >why I still believe they are external. I cant seem to caulk my ear
> and
> > > >tell
> > > > >which direction the tones are coming from.
> > > >
> > > >Right, that's characteristic of low-frequency sound perception. You
can
> > > >confirm that by connecting only a subwoofer speaker to your stereo,
> > closing
> > > >your eyes, then trying to determine the speaker location. You'll find
> > it's
> > > >difficult to localize unless you sense pressure waves directly with
> your
> > > >body. At higher frequencies, the geometry of the ears and the phase
> > > >difference (time delay) of sound reaching the two ears, along with
> > > >frequency
> > > >attentation differences (high frequencies will be reduced in one ear
if
> > > >they
> > > >originate on the opposite side of the head), along with room
> reflections,
> > > >all provide cues that the human acoustic system uses at higher
> > frequencies
> > > >to localize sound. That's why you can focus on one conversation in a
> > > >crowded
> > > >room (the "cocktail party effect"). So it's reasonable (I don't have
a
> > > >reference to support this, so consider it informed speculation) to
> assume
> > > >that thermoelastic-generating sound (converted from RF) within the
> skull
> > > >would sound identical to sound originating from outside, since
outside
> > > >sound
> > > >lacks localization cues, especially that portion that travels to the
> > > >cochlea
> > > >via bone conduction in the head (bone conduction is higher at lower
> > > >frequencies), where there are no localization cues from the outer
ear.
> > > >Bottom line: the sounds you hear are most likely endogenous
(generated
> > > >inside your head, either by RF, some anomaly in your acoustic system
> > > >creating artifacts, or some other process). Another possibility is
that
> > you
> > > >are hearing exogenous (externally generated) sounds generated by some
> > other
> > > >process (not RF).
> > > >
> > > >I hope all that makes sense? Scott may want to review that for
> accuracy.
> > > >
> > > > >was actually feeling the broadcast!!! The surface of my skin felt
> > > >slightly
> > > > >tingly, like the hairs standing up, I looked at my arms and the
hairs
> > > >were
> > > > >not extended
> > > >
> > > >There are at least two possibilities here:
> > > >
> > > >1. You were sensing a high-voltage 60 Hz power line. Humans perceive
60
> > Hz
> > > >electric fields greater than approximately 15 kV/m (kilovolts per
> meter)
> > as
> > > >"tingling" caused by vibration of hairs [1, p. 355]. (Note: the
safety
> > > >limit
> > > >for exposure to electric fields from high-voltage power lines is 4 to
> 10
> > > >kV/m [1, p. 466], depending on which standard, so you were risking
> shock
> > > >from induced current and should avoid that area.) This is the most
> likely
> > > >explanation. How far from high voltage power lines in the area were
you
> > > >standing? These high-voltage lines would be required to provide the
> power
> > > >to
> > > >drive the high-power 192 kW NLK transmitter.
> > > >
> > > >2. You were sensing the 24 kHz signal directly. I don't know of any
> > > >research
> > > >regarding sensing frequencies in that range with body hairs, so my
best
> > > >speculation is that explanation #1 above is more likely. I'd like to
be
> > > >proved wrong on this.
> > > >
> > > > >but the force was penetrating my body, definitely bombarding it
> > > > > as if I were in a strong magnetic field.
> > > >
> > > >Could you be more specific about what your sensations were? The only
> > > >mechanism
> > > >we have for sensing magnetic fields is visual phosphenes (the "stars
in
> > > >your
> > > >eyes" visual effect you get when you rub your eyes vigorously or get
> hit
> > in
> > > >the head), caused by magnetic stimulation of the retina [1, p. 387],
so
> > > >unless you saw "stars" that's not likely.

> > > > >Right, that's characteristic of low-frequency sound perception. You

> > > closing
> > > > >your eyes, then trying to determine the speaker location. You'll
find
> > > it's
> > > > >difficult to localize unless you sense pressure waves directly with
> > your
> > > > >body. At higher frequencies, the geometry of the ears and the phase
> > > > >difference (time delay) of sound reaching the two ears, along with
> > > > >frequency
> > > > >attentation differences (high frequencies will be reduced in one
ear
> if
> > > > >they
> > > > >originate on the opposite side of the head), along with room
> > reflections,
> > > > >all provide cues that the human acoustic system uses at higher
> > > frequencies
> > > > >to localize sound. That's why you can focus on one conversation in
a
> > > > >crowded
> > > > >room (the "cocktail party effect"). So it's reasonable (I don't
have
> a
> > > > >reference to support this, so consider it informed speculation) to
> > assume
> > > > >that thermoelastic-generating sound (converted from RF) within the
> > skull
> > > > >would sound identical to sound originating from outside, since
> outside
> > > > >sound
> > > > >lacks localization cues, especially that portion that travels to
the
> > > > >cochlea
> > > > >via bone conduction in the head (bone conduction is higher at lower
> > > > >frequencies), where there are no localization cues from the outer
> ear.
> > > > >Bottom line: the sounds you hear are most likely endogenous
> (generated
> > > > >inside your head, either by RF, some anomaly in your acoustic
system
> > > > >creating artifacts, or some other process). Another possibility is
> that
> > > you
> > > > >are hearing exogenous (externally generated) sounds generated by
some
> > > other

SCOTT ANDREW KLABIS wrote:

> Yes: the key here to high frequency components is the NON-LINEAR
> device.  As a high current low frequency wave conducts through
> such a semi-conducting device or oxidized connection a transient
> signal is produced by said non-linear e/i characteristics.  As
> an example, a standard silicone diode conducts in one direction
> at a threshold of about .7 volts.  If a low frequency source is
> capable of producing a voltage greater than this, the resultant
> angle of the vector into said conduction represents a smaller
> period in time than would occur in a pure sinusoid.
>
> Regarding biological sensititvity, I would guess the synaptic
> terminals of a neuron might function in ways like a diode, but
> my primary concern lies in an entirely different sphere yielding
> to theory that magnetic fields (perpendicular to static fields)
> physically agitate iron oxide in hemoglobin... have yet to see
> much of anything published to this effect but thanks the same
> for references..

hi Doug,

a few suggestions: you might be hearing some interference patterns which means
that the output of the sine generator (which I assume is a clean sinewave in
your case) mixes with other back ground noises like your computer fan, fridge
compressor etc. Also if you used speakers there might be standing waves inside
your listening room, the quality of the amplifier is not up to scratch, so you
might hear interference products/distortions caused by power supply ripple etc.

Therefore I suggest using the generator in a really quiet room on a battery
powered laptop if possible and only through head phones.
cheers, Peter.

know in modern biology that red cells of human blood contains iron 
oxide, and by laws of physical science we know that iron oxide is a 
magnetically permiable substance.  The attraction/repulsion resulting
from magnetic (north/south) orientation of such SYNTHETIC molecules 
has attributed to applications in magnetic tape and computer disk
memory-storage for many years.

reputable or popular) conducted studies suggesting that telepathic
communications depended upon magnetic lines of force.  In later years

sub-consious mechanism.  Unfortunately, however, in a day when freedom
of speech prevails above and beyond an otherwise mandated whole truth

Hi Dorothy,

You might be slow on the technological end but nevertheless you are curious
enough and ready to learn - a very very nice and important trait indeed. I am
glad you picked this up since I was waiting for someone to come forward with this
question! But please let me mention first, that the following method was posted
to me by list member Dr. Franz Frosch.

The purpose of the experiment is to measure the perceived hum frequency with a
strikingly high accuracy.

What you need:
a high quality battery driven sine wave generator - alternatively a battery
powered laptop PC with a sound card running a software implemented sine wave
generator, a reasonably good quality set of head(ear) phones, a quiet (and I mean
as quiet as possible) listening environment and finally of course THE HUM!

Tune the sinewave generator to a frequency range of 40...100 Hz and let it sweep
through this range within 20 seconds or so. Just get the hang of the frequency
generator by turning its dials, volume control etc. Then try to decrease the
output volume to the point where you can hardly hear the pure sinusoidal tones.
You'll notice that the threshold of hearing the tones is lower at the higher end
(100 Hz in this example) - this is because the sensitivity of the ear rolls off
by going low in frequency. As you sweep through the lower end of your hearing
range, compare the tones with the hum frequency. This way you should be able to
roughly tell if the generated tones are above or below the hum frequency. Once
this is established, narrow the sweep range from 40...100 Hz to a range with just
covers the hum frequency (you should be able to narrow it down to a few Hz).
Make sure the volume for this narrow range is just above the threshold of
hearing. Now you decrease the sweeping speed down to about 40 seconds or so. The
output of the tone generator now slowly increases the frequency to the dialed
upper frequency and then loops back and starts again at the lower frequency,
continuing the cycle. If the sweep window covers the hum frequency you'll notice
some interference in the form of beating. It's a bit like tuning a string
instrument. The closer the tones get to the hum frequency the slower the beating.
This works for both higher and lower end. So f.e. if your hum were at 71.3 Hz
you'd be able to count the same number of beats per minute at 69.3 Hz as at 73.3
Hz. With a bit of practice you'll be able to very accurately determine the
frequency at which you perceive the hum.
Please feel free to ask questions.
BTW there are some pitfalls in every individual setup of the experiment which
need careful attention.
cheers, Peter.

Wednesday July 4 10:58 PM ET
U.S. Missile Defense Protest Ends

LONDON (AP) - Demonstrators who occupied part of a British radar base
surrendered to police late Wednesday, ending a two-day protest against a
proposed U.S. missile defense system.

The last two protesters descended from a radio mast inside the Menwith Hill
military base in North Yorkshire at 10 p.m. and surrendered to police,
according to the environmental group Greenpeace.

Greenpeace claims that base is one of two in Britain the U.S. military would
need in order to be the ``eyes and ears'' of President Bush (news - web
sites)'s missile defense system.

On Tuesday, about 100 protesters stormed inside the base's fenced-in
grounds. Most were evicted later that day. By Wednesday afternoon, only two
protesters remained inside. It was not immediately clear if there would be
any charges filed against the protesters.

``The whole purpose of this event was to expose the role that Britain will
play in the Star Wars program and we have done that to great effect,'' said
Greenpeace protester Andy Tait.

Well ... not much of a riot .. G.D. did you for get L.A? Now thats a riot!

http://www.guardian.co.uk/Archive/Article/0,4273,4216915,00.html

Greenpeace strikes back

Andy Tait, 30, is a Greenpeace campaigner who occupied a roof for 20 hours
at RAF Menwith Hill, near Harrogate, which houses the vital link in the
£100bn star wars system.

Amy Fleming
Guardian

Friday July 6, 2001


This project was three months in the planning and I spent the weekend in the
office making last-minute preparations. As many as 130 people - around 20
Greenpeace staff and the rest were supporters from around the country - were
to invade the base.

My team of 40 were to break in through three main access gates and on Monday
we had a run-through in a field. It felt like a scene from It's a Knockout.
The MoD claimed that we had developed amazingly technical equipment to gain
entry but in fact we used household ladders.

We woke up at 3am on Tuesday and sat on the coach in silence with our
adrenalin pumping, travelling to one of the most secure military bases in
the UK. We feared we'd get arrested before we even got there - even if we
did get in, we had no idea what would happen next.

Luckily we had a completely clean run at it. It was only when we were inside
that we saw a guard but, alone, all he could do was ask us to stop and track
us as we went further into the base. About 25 of us climbed on to a roof,
about 35-40ft high, near the two star wars infrared missile-tracking sys
tems, armed with snack bars, fruit, sun cream, a first-aid kit and chains
(to make the action more sustainable). We also had shortwave radios to keep
in touch with fellow protesters, and mobile phones. It was incredibly odd
sitting on a roof in a high-security base talking to a radio station in
south-east Asia. I spent a good deal of the day doing interviews with people
all over the world including New Zealand, Australia, Denmark, Canada and
even British Forces Broadcasting.

The guards were fairly light-hearted as they knew they weren't in any
danger. The guy circling us with a dog looked up periodically to check we
were OK, and to make sure we had sun protection. It's a tough situation for
them as they have to take into account our safety and their own when
removing us. They decided to get a rope access team in but having first
dealt with the water-tower team, they didn't get us down until about 1am.
They built scaffolding, climbed on to the roof, brought us down one by one,
put us in the back of an MoD van and dumped us outside the front gate.

We could have been done for trespass or criminal damage but only the six
they caught painting were actually arrested. We piled into our Luton van and
arrived at our hostel at around 3am, trying to find empty beds in the dark
until someone woke up and pointed us in the right direction.

On Wednesday I was back outside the base doing support work for people who
had managed to get in again. This mostly involved sitting around drinking
lots of coffee. We liaised between the protesters and the press and police
when they tried to negotiate with demonstrators. The protesters eventually
had to come down at 10pm because they had run out of water.

That night, exhausted, we found a hotel and slept well. I spent Thursday
morning sitting in the sun recovering before returning to London for a
planning meeting. I think I'll try and take a long weekend.

>
According to your experience/expertise, what kind of listening setup would be
required to get the tones below 20 Hz across?
<
Well, at the acoustics lab here a small airtight closet (=box) is used. The
person is enclosed in the closet, and the walls of the closet are covered with
large diameter bass or woofer loudspeaker units. This an expensive and
scientifically correct way of generating infrasound (sound with frequencies
below 20 Hz) in a controllable way, and making the infrasound heard by the
person.

I have been using Sennheiser HD265 closed headphones which have a frequency
range which extends below 20 Hz. With these I can generate infrasound which can
be heard by most persons. I have found that it is common among hum sufferers to
be extremely sensitive to infrasound.

I have also found that infrasound and lowfrequency is common in dwellings, and
in the dwellings of hum sufferers. The sound pressure levels are high enough to
be heard by extremely sensitive individuals.

The infrasound in dwellings cannot easily be picked up by low cost electret
microphones for two reasons. One reason is that the low cost microphone
generates a background noise which is roughly inversely proportional to the
frequency. So the microphone background noise is predominantly a low
frequency/infrasound rumble, which tends to mask the infrasound noise in the
dwelling. To get a clean recording of low frequency noise you have to use a low
noise microphone. A bass loudspeaker unit is commonly used as a microphone if
you want low cost, and if you dont care about the poor frequency and phase
response of the loudspeaker unit (compared to condensor microphones).

>
I assume you'd have to use high
wattage headphones to prevent sound pressure waves being felt by other body
parts
which then might be confused with "hearing" the tones?
<
It is generally considered that the inner ear is the most sensitive body part
for infrasound, so you dont need to protect other body parts. But you may need
to protect the inner ear from vibrations, which may be picked up, and perceived
as acoustic sound.


>
In my opinion sound waves in
this low frequency range are simply not a candidate for carrying the hum.
<
Well, I disagree...

>
Did you get a chance to measure your perceived hum frequency as yet?
<
Ï havent followed the recent discussion on hum frequencies here, but
I have tried to measure hum frequencies many times, as I have described before.
I usually arrive at the frequency interval 10-50 Hz. Especially 17 and 25 Hz or
49 Hz.

Rergards, Anders

hello Anders,

apparently you do have access to fairly high quality testing/laboratory equipment.
What is your procedure when measuring your own or anybody else's hum?

As to the sensitivity of electrets:
they do produce their fair share of self noise but nevertheless they are also
capable of picking up infra sound.
Even if the self noise would start to drown out the infrasound signal (perhaps at
S/N <3dB?) the signal would still be detectable by means of an FFT processor. In my
own experiments I have generated infrasound waves of about 8 Hz which are picked up
by my cheap electret mic with a S/N of about 10....16 dB. This produces a prominent
reading on the FFT as well as on the CRO of course.
Another interesting aspect is comparing different sound levels/frequencies. In my
environment it is easy to record low frequency signals from idling car engines in
the distance. If I compare the recorded noise from the engines to what I hear, I
must say that the electret makes low intensity sound visible on my PC screen before
it gets loud enough for me to hear it. I am talking about frequencies between
30....75 Hz here.
Another example of comparative listening: there is a fridge compressor humming away
with a fundamental of 48 Hz which I cannot hear up here in the first floor (fridge
is on the ground floor), the FFT makes the 48 Hz visible though with a S/N of >10
dB. From this I conclude that my cheap electret is suitable for low frequency sound
hunting. Of course these mics are not suitable for "clean" recordings due to their
bad self noise specs as you already indicated, but all we need to make them do is
picking up traces of the low stuff......

I have a very simple experiment for you:

Take your closed Sennheisers, put an electret into the enclosure between your ear
and the inner wall of one of the headphones and start listening to low
intensity/low frequency tones while you monitor the feedback from the electret.
Please let me know the result (as to the electrets ability to picking up the tones
before you hear anything).

regards, Peter.

>
Please let me know the result (as to the electrets ability to picking up the
tones
before you hear anything).
<

Pure tones are easily detected by FFT techniques through random noise. I have
picked up weak signals with electrets using FFT techniques that I could not pick
up with my ears.

The ears do not have the same ability to pick out pure tones from background
noise at low frequencies, so the ears need a cleaner recording in order to be
able to recognize a pure tone hum in the recording. In my experience electret
microphones do not give a sufficiently clean recording, and the person will be
unable to recognize his hum from a recording made by electret microphones.

S/N ratios given can be misleading when it is not stated how they are computed.
A S/N ratio mentioned in connetion with FFT analysis is probably computed from a
narrow frequency interval, which would not be the relevant S/N ratio for human
hearing. For human hearing it is more relevant to compare the total
energycontent of the recording with the energycontent of the signal. Perhaps
frequency-weighted to compensate for the frequency-response of the ear.

When you have made a recording from which the hum can be recognized, and when
this recording is clean in the sense that the total energy content of the
background noise is less than 1/10 of the energy content of the hum, then you
have a good basis for analyzing the hum, and finding characteristic frequencies
in it.

If the hum can be recognized on the recording it is however not a total proof
that the hum heard by the person is identical to the hum recorded.

Regards, Anders

Anders wrote:.......................

totally agreed.

Anders also says ...................I have
picked up weak signals with electrets using FFT techniques that I could not pick
up with my ears....................

This matches precisely my own experience which I expressed in my previous posting in
this thread.
In other words, if the FFT doesn't show up any traces of hum as picked up by the
microphone then there is no hum in the frequency band under investigation -  how
should the ear pick out something which doesn't even show up on the FFT which does a
better job on it?

This brings us back to my conclusion that cheap electret microphones are
sufficiently sensitive in the low frequency band for picking up and showing on FFT
any suspicious frequencies which might carry the audible hum. If the microphone/FFT
don't show anything then there just ain't no sound waves carrying the hum.

Now finally may I ask you again how you measured your perceived hum frequency?

> Please let me know the result (as to the electrets ability to picking up the
> tones
> before you hear anything).
> <
>
> Pure tones are easily detected by FFT techniques through random noise. I have
> picked up weak signals with electrets using FFT techniques that I could not pick
> up with my ears.
>
> The ears do not have the same ability to pick out pure tones from background
> noise at low frequencies, so the ears need a cleaner recording in order to be
> able to recognize a pure tone hum in the recording. In my experience electret
> microphones do not give a sufficiently clean recording, and the person will be
> unable to recognize his hum from a recording made by electret microphones.
>
> S/N ratios given can be misleading when it is not stated how they are computed.
> A S/N ratio mentioned in connetion with FFT analysis is probably computed from a
> narrow frequency interval, which would not be the relevant S/N ratio for human
> hearing. For human hearing it is more relevant to compare the total
> energycontent of the recording with the energycontent of the signal. Perhaps
> frequency-weighted to compensate for the frequency-response of the ear.
>
> When you have made a recording from which the hum can be recognized, and when
> this recording is clean in the sense that the total energy content of the
> background noise is less than 1/10 of the energy content of the hum, then you
> have a good basis for analyzing the hum, and finding characteristic frequencies
> in it.
>
> If the hum can be recognized on the recording it is however not a total proof
> that the hum heard by the person is identical to the hum recorded.
>
> Regards, Anders

I am generally concerned with sine waves for the following reason:
anything else than sine waves has overtones which would be better audible than
the fundamental because of the ear's better sensitivity in the higher regions.

generation of a beat-frequency between the two ears.

ok Anders,

could it be that the hum signal which doesn't show up as a peak is a band of pink
noise? The ear then kind of averages the sound energy/frequencies in this band and
gives the impression of "a tone"....At one stage when I discovered these bands of
environmental noise I was thinking along these lines. But when I looked at the
intensity of the noise in these bands which vary quite a bit from hour to hour, I
did not find a correlation with the loudness of my hum.
This observation however still offers some food for thought and maybe validates
future experiments.

Now if you are able to listen to the hum in real time through filters then you are
able to record it!

May I offer my thoughts about filtering for discussion:
If you get any microphone, amplify its output and then tune any bandpass filter to
any frequency band, you will hear tones which match the filter's pass band
frequencies.
All you basically do is create a band of pink noise out of the "white" output noise
band from the microphone. The sum of all spectral components being passed by the
filter becomes smaller by narrowing the passband  hence the output becomes more and
more sinusoidal but also looses the intensity of a wide open loud and noisy band
pass.

The question is, how do you arrive at the band pass' center frequency? What lets you
decide where you tune your filter to? There is no doubt that the filter tuning will
determine your hum frequency.....The problem is that you have to amplify a signal
(plus the self noise of the mic and the amplifier itself) which you then squeeze
through a filter.....

What do you think about Dr. Frosch' method which involves no recording or
amplification of minute acoustic signals (if there were any) at all and allows the
hum frequency being measured with a resolution in the order of a tenth of a Hertz?

cheers, Peter.

ok Anders,

you said you are using band pass filters and then you gradually narrow down the pass
band, right?
What lets you decide where the centre frequency of your filter is, 75 Hz, 15 Hz or
any other frequency?
I mean if you listened to the hum then gradually narrow the pass band of a band pass
in order to arrive at the hum frequency then you'd have to know the hum frequency
beforehand.....
Especially in light of the possibility that the hum is pink noise then this method
would give you any frequency inside the pink noise band as a candidate for the
hum...its just up to yourself to which centre frequency you tune your filter, what
do you need your filter for then?

Anyway, Dr. Frosch' method works regardless of the hum being acoustic in nature or
RF or else....
I'd like you to try it, evaluate it and let me know the result. I have attached the
method for you so you don't have to search for it in the archive (or in your email
inbox).
******************************************************
The purpose of the experiment is to measure the perceived hum frequency with a
strikingly high accuracy.

What you need:
a high quality battery driven sine wave generator - alternatively a battery
powered laptop PC with a sound card running a software implemented sine wave
generator, a reasonably good quality set of head(ear) phones, a quiet (and I mean
as quiet as possible) listening environment and finally of course THE HUM!

Tune the sinewave generator to a frequency range of 40...100 Hz and let it sweep
through this range within 20 seconds or so. Just get the hang of the frequency
generator by turning its dials, volume control etc. Then try to decrease the
output volume to the point where you can hardly hear the pure sinusoidal tones.
You'll notice that the threshold of hearing the tones is lower at the higher end
(100 Hz in this example) - this is because the sensitivity of the ear rolls off
by going low in frequency. As you sweep through the lower end of your hearing
range, compare the tones with the hum frequency. This way you should be able to
roughly tell if the generated tones are above or below the hum frequency. Once
this is established, narrow the sweep range from 40...100 Hz to a range with just
covers the hum frequency (you should be able to narrow it down to a few Hz).
Make sure the volume for this narrow range is just above the threshold of
hearing. Now you decrease the sweeping speed down to about 40 seconds or so. The
output of the tone generator now slowly increases the frequency to the dialed
upper frequency and then loops back and starts again at the lower frequency,
continuing the cycle. If the sweep window covers the hum frequency you'll notice
some interference in the form of beating. It's a bit like tuning a string
instrument. The closer the tones get to the hum frequency the slower the beating.
This works for both higher and lower end. So f.e. if your hum were at 71.3 Hz
you'd be able to count the same number of beats per minute at 69.3 Hz as at 73.3
Hz. With a bit of practice you'll be able to very accurately determine the
frequency at which you perceive the hum.
Please feel free to ask questions.
BTW there are some pitfalls in every individual setup of the experiment which
need careful attention.
*********************************************************

cheers, Peter.

result of internal thermal heating, or if it is exogenous, coming from

until I can prove otherwise)therefore, my proposed solution would be to 
build a device that would produce the opposite frequency, or "White" noise.

are hearing, then build a device to produce the opposite frequency. This 
white noise application already exists in cars to produce a better ride by 
eliminating road noise.We have some common ground to work with here, but the 
task of doing as I propose seems to be slightly overwhelming, for me 
anyway.I need to do 2 things... try to tape record the tones I hear, and 
secondly,obtain a sine wave generator to identify and mimick the tones.In my 
first step , if I can record the tones, would prove that the tones are 
coming from outside my head!!! I would be exstatic if I could do that. This 
would still lead me to the next step of wanting to visualize the tones on an 
oscilliscope, THEN reproduce the tones with electronics or musical 
instruments in relationship to the musical scale. That should keep me busy 
till dinner time!!!!! Take care. Rick

Rick,

your concept is interesting and commonly known as active noise cancellation.
Active noise cancellation however works best with loud noise signals. Another
pre requisite for ANC is that you have to have sound waves (the hum has to be
acoustic in nature) which you then can try to cancel out by producing "opposite"
sound waves with a 180 degree phase shift.

BTW if you listen to externally generated tones which are close to your
perceived hum then you create rhythmic periods of "noise cancellation" which you
then hear as beating.

cheers, Peter.

Hi Anders,

you wrote:..................................

I have tried a method similar to Dr. Frosch'. I can get beat frequencies, but I
get several beat frequencies at harmonics or subharmonics of the hum signal
frequency, so I don't like the method. I find that it can be misleading. With
the hum signals here, it is often difficult to get beat frequencies with good
certainty................................................

This again lets me think that your hum is a band of low frequency noise - similar
to airborne city noise heard from a distance.
Otherwise, if the hum were a single wave then the beating experiment would be the
best way for determining the hum frequency.
Even if your hum wave would be non sinusoidal with a lot of harmonics then you'd
still get the strongest beating at the frequency which is the most audible one
(probably the hum frequency).
If for some reason you think that this is not the fundamental frequency of the hum,
all you'd have to do is repeat the beating experiment at 1/3, 1/5, 1/7 etc. of this
frequency and listen for beatings.
I have an idea what you could mean by "subharmonics" but still would like to know
what you call a subharmonic.

Final questions:
from what I heard from you so far, your hum seems to be pink noise.
What do you use filtering for, and what are the the corner frequencies of your band
pass when you tune in to your hum? Where is the band of pink noise in the audible
spectrum, which you seem to hold responsible for the hum?

cheers, Peter.

> Hi Dorothy,

what is a wave and what is a pulse you asked?

in the context of sound I would say a wave is energy which gets passed on from a
group of air molecules to the next group. The molecules themselves oscillate (go
back and forth) around their normal stable point in space. The simplest way for
the molecules to do this is to oscillate like a pendulum which represents a sine.
The amount (amplitude) by which the molecules move up and down determines the
sound intensity, the number of ups and downs per second determine the frequency
of the sound. In case of pure tones the movement of these molecules is always
sinusoidal which is the simplest form of an oscillation. More complex composite
sound waves  involve a number of sinewaves (all multiples of the base sound wave)
acting upon the molecules as a combined deflecting force hence the molecule's
movements are not pure sine anymore.

A pulse I would say is the passing on of energy by the acceleration of air
molecules beyond the normal speed of sound which prevents a wavelike behaviour -
the molecules do not oscillate around their normal point in space and do not
interact with the neighboring group of molecules in a wavelike fashion. Examples
for pulses are all kinds of shockwaves caused by explosions or other supersonic
objects moving through air and accelerating air molecules beyond the speed of
sound. Pulses carry a lot more energy than sound waves. Other examples for pulses
f.e. in water are Tsunamis, or EMPs caused by nuclear explosions.
I hope this helps a bit.
cheers, Peter.
