Wes,

I always use pure sine waves.

If the infrasonic sound waves are complex and loud enough (rich in overtones)
than yes, they would be audible. I assume that the second and fourth overtones
(fundamental x3 and x5) would be the most audible ones, maybe the 6th as well
because of the increased sensitivity of the ear in the higher region. My hum is
at about 71.5 Hz which would mean that if this were an overtone then the
fundamental of the hum (if carried by sound) could be at 23.83, at 14.3, at
10.2, at 7.94 etc. Hz. If my hum would be induced by RF then there would be
additional fundamental frequencies possible like the ones at 71.5/2, 71.5/4,
71.5/2 etc.

If I remember right, in my earlier experiments with electrets and speaker boxes
I came across noise bands centered around 25 Hz and 75 Hz. No significant lines
showed up on the spectrum though. This would mean that the audible hum could be
an average of the second overtones originating from the (in my opinion
relatively inaudible) noise band around 25 Hz or even from the fourth overtones
from a band around 15 Hz which I then paid no attention to.

I guess I will have to make further experiments soon.....

regards, Peter.

>
Peter: To state my question more clearly: I'm interested in finding out if
infrasonic pulsed signals below the hearing range might be audible only
because of their high-frequency components (transients, harmonics,
intermodulation), whereas sine-wave signal of the same frequency would not

Probably.

It is known that high frequency components above 20 kHz, which cannot be heard
when they occur alone, can be heard when they are accompanied by lower frequency
components below 20 kHz.

Something similar possibly occurs at infrasound frequencies. The human ear is a
rather non-linear device, and it will react to a sum of two frequencies in a
nonlinear way.

Regards, Anders

Not to complicate things, but to elaborate on the distinction
of "sine" waves from "pulse" waves, a sine wave as shown on the
screen of an oscilloscope or graphed on paper is a representation
of a change in current, voltage or physical motion produced by a
"rotating" source.  The reason it is called a sine wave is becuase
such representation is derived in real time from the sine of the
angles of the wave as it rotates.  A prime example of a sine wave 
would be the type of alternating current produced by a rotating 
generator, or also by the transposition to a circular plane (in
position verses time) the motion created by a swinging pendulum 
or a vibrating reed, etc.. . 

A "pulse" wave, on the other hand, represents a spontanious change
in voltage, current or other energy which does not necessarily have
such circular repetition characteristics.  Examples of pulse waves 
(in addition to those cited by Peter) might be the transient wave
produced by switch contacts opening or closing.  Electrical "noise"
is a prime example of random opening and closing of gaps between
current carriers due to poor electrical contact.  Often these kinds
of waves show up as a series of random pulses. 

	S. Klabis / sak55@aztec.asu.edu

>
>> Hi Dorothy,
>
>what is a wave and what is a pulse you asked?
>
>in the context of sound I would say a wave is energy which gets passed on from a
>group of air molecules to the next group. The molecules themselves oscillate (go
>back and forth) around their normal stable point in space. The simplest way for
>the molecules to do this is to oscillate like a pendulum which represents a sine.
>The amount (amplitude) by which the molecules move up and down determines the
>sound intensity, the number of ups and downs per second determine the frequency
>of the sound. In case of pure tones the movement of these molecules is always
>sinusoidal which is the simplest form of an oscillation. More complex composite
>sound waves  involve a number of sinewaves (all multiples of the base sound wave)
>acting upon the molecules as a combined deflecting force hence the molecule's
>movements are not pure sine anymore.
>
>A pulse I would say is the passing on of energy by the acceleration of air
>molecules beyond the normal speed of sound which prevents a wavelike behaviour -
>the molecules do not oscillate around their normal point in space and do not
>interact with the neighboring group of molecules in a wavelike fashion. Examples
>for pulses are all kinds of shockwaves caused by explosions or other supersonic
>objects moving through air and accelerating air molecules beyond the speed of
>sound. Pulses carry a lot more energy than sound waves. Other examples for pulses
>f.e. in water are Tsunamis, or EMPs caused by nuclear explosions.
>I hope this helps a bit.
>cheers, Peter.
>

> return home.One would think that our cranial tissue would become agitated
> enough to bring out other symptoms

Not likely:

1. The brain has no internal pain sensors.

2. If Chou's theory is correct (and it has general support of scientists at
this time), RF hearing (the idea that brain can convert pulsed
radio-frequency signals to audible sounds via thermoelastic expansion of
brain tissues, causing an audible internal shock wave) would have extremely
minimal effects on the brain -- only one millionth of a degree centigrade,
in other words, a million times weaker than the brain-temperature elevation
effects of a slight fever from the flu:

"The threshold of hearing was determined to be approximately 10
microjoule/gm per pulse, which causes an increment of temperature in the
head of one millionth of a degree centigrade!"
http://www.electric-words.com/cell/research/laisingh/memory1.html

The next part of that paragraph, though is very interesting:

"Lebovitz [1975] gives another example of a microthermal effect of RFR on
the vestibulocochlear apparatus, an organ in the inner ear responsible for
keeping body balance and sensing of movement. He proposed that an uneven
distribution of RFR absorption in the head can set up a temperature gradient
in the semicircular canals, which in turns affect the function of the
vestibular system."

This suggests a possible diagnostic for RF hearing: a vestibular system
test, which is sometimes down in conjuntion with a hearing test. Question:
do hummers notice any loss of balance, which would partially (but not
definitively) support the RF hearing hypothesis?

Hi Wes,

you said:............
In addition to overtones, there may also be beat/intermodulation frequencies
(as aheerfor@sca.csc.com pointed out) and transients at random frequencies
due to pulse rise/decay components. The frequent "idling deisel" description
also suggests pulsed sounds rather than sine waves..............

Wes, as to my understanding (brought to me by French scientist Mr. Fourier) ALL
sound waves are a mixture of sine waves (and their phase shifted buddies called
cosines). Any transients appearing in a low tone momentarily add additional
sinewaves to the tone. These transients can be a multiple of the fundamental
(overtones) or if they are not an overtone then they potentially interfere with
the lower tone which is sometimes called intermodulation. Intermodulation
becomes possible in a non linear environment at the source of the tones or
inside the pickup unit (microphone or ear). Intermodulation produces new
frequencies. If two tones of 1kHz and 90Hz would start to intermodulate in a non
linear fashion inside the ear (in case the 90 Hz is a loud tone f.e.) then the
additional new frequencies you'd hear are 900 Hz and 1100Hz. These new
frequencies are not externally measurable unless intermodulation already takes
place at the sound source (like in an overdriven speaker membrane where the high
bass amplitudes intermodulate with lower amplitude high frequency tones).
This out of the way, back to our hum problem. We are concerned with low energy
low frequency tones (or noise). If these tones were intermodulation products of
other tones then it is apparent that these are the higher frequency product of
the intermodulation (like the 1100Hz in the example above). In my case the
higher frequency of this (for this matter intermodulation product) is around
71.5 Hz. So if there were any infrasonic sound generating intermodulation
products then one of the original (real) frequency components would be somewhere
below 20 Hz. Say at 10 Hz. Then the other original (real) frequency in the
equation would need to be at 81.5 Hz. Intermodulation of 10 Hz and 81.5 gives
the new (audible but unmeasurable if intermodulation takes place in the ear
only) frequencies of 71.5 Hz and 91.5 Hz.
Now I am asking you: why do I hear the 71.5 Hz and not the 91.5 and not the
external (loud) 81.5 Hz, why don't microphones pick up the 81.5 Hz nor the 10 Hz
or any other loud tones in this range which could be part of the equation?
The answer is simple: because the hum is not an acoustic intermodulation
product.

And now to your repeated mentioning of pulses and transients.
Pulses (I assume these are sharp rises of air pressure?) and transients (I
assume these are fast events?) always create a long trail of harmonics in
connection with sound. These long trails of harmonics carry over into the better
audible range. If my hum would be accompanied by pulses or transients then these
would be heard much louder than the steady low rumble of the hum.
If the pulses and transients are brought into the context with infrasonic sound
(everything is relative) then there would be a trail of harmonics rising up from
the infrasonic range. F.e. if there would be transients happening around 8 Hz
then there would be at least a harmonic at 24, 40, 56, 72.....Hz. Weaker
overtones could also be observed at the even multiples of the fundamental of 8
Hz. Why then is it that I only hear a 0.5 to a few Hz amplitude modulated 71.5
Hz tone and nothing else?
The answer is simple: because there are no transients happening at 8 Hz or
thereabout.

BTW I did extensive measurements in the infrasonic range with an electret
microphone inside my house. The amount of airpressure fluctuations as picked up
by the microphone, caused by the slightest breeze outside the house is
tremendous. These fluctuations cause sound waves with a frequency up to 10 Hz
with amplitudes 100 times higher than say my fridge compressor at 48 Hz measured
from a distance of one metre.
Within a metre listening distance from the fridge I can just barely hear the
fundamental of 48 Hz because it gets drowned out by its harmonics, but I never
managed to hear the infrasonic waves created by winds of ANY strength.........

Please note that the sound energy arriving at the eardrum required to hear
something at 20 Hz needs to be about 100 million times higher compared to the
energy required at 3.5 kHz.
So if we are talking about hearing low frequency acoustic waves, we are not
talking about chickenfeed, there is quite a bit of energy in audible soundwaves
in this low frequency range hence relatively easy picked up by electret
microphones (which do not have the significant sensitivity rolloff of the human
ear which starts at about 700 Hz).

I hope for all of you who are curious enough to follow my thoughts about my
perceived hum, the above offers some insight.
Please send me your feedback if you think that I am wrong in one of the aspects
or assumptions.
Also, I'd like to invite everybody else who has done measurements to come
forward with his/her results. Have you done any measurements yourself Wes? If
yes, please let us know.

regards, Peter.

the new (audible but unmeasurable if intermodulation takes place in the
ear
only) frequencies of 71.5 Hz and 91.5 Hz.
Now I am asking you: why do I hear the 71.5 Hz and not the 91.5 and not
the
external (loud) 81.5 Hz, why don't microphones pick up the 81.5 Hz nor
the 10 Hz
or any other loud tones in this range which could be part of the
equation?
The answer is simple: because the hum is not an acoustic intermodulation

product.

And now to your repeated mentioning of pulses and transients.
Pulses (I assume these are sharp rises of air pressure?) and transients
(I
assume these are fast events?) always create a long trail of harmonics
in
connection with sound. These long trails of harmonics carry over into
the better
audible range. If my hum would be accompanied by pulses or transients
then these
would be heard much louder than the steady low rumble of the hum.
If the pulses and transients are brought into the context with
infrasonic sound
(everything is relative) then there would be a trail of harmonics rising
up from
the infrasonic range. F.e. if there would be transients happening around
8 Hz
then there would be at least a harmonic at 24, 40, 56, 72.....Hz. Weaker

overtones could also be observed at the even multiples of the
fundamental of 8
Hz. Why then is it that I only hear a 0.5 to a few Hz amplitude
modulated 71.5
Hz tone and nothing else?
The answer is simple: because there are no transients happening at 8 Hz
or
thereabout.

BTW I did extensive measurements in the infrasonic range with an
electret
microphone inside my house. The amount of airpressure fluctuations as
picked up
by the microphone, caused by the slightest breeze outside the house is
tremendous. These fluctuations cause sound waves with a frequency up to
10 Hz
with amplitudes 100 times higher than say my fridge compressor at 48 Hz
measured
from a distance of one metre.
Within a metre listening distance from the fridge I can just barely hear
the
fundamental of 48 Hz because it gets drowned out by its harmonics, but I
never
managed to hear the infrasonic waves created by winds of ANY
strength.........

Please note that the sound energy arriving at the eardrum required to
hear
something at 20 Hz needs to be about 100 million times higher compared
to the
energy required at 3.5 kHz.
So if we are talking about hearing low frequency acoustic waves, we are
not
talking about chickenfeed, there is quite a bit of energy in audible
soundwaves
in this low frequency range hence relatively easy picked up by electret
microphones (which do not have the significant sensitivity rolloff of
the human
ear which starts at about 700 Hz).

I hope for all of you who are curious enough to follow my thoughts about
my
perceived hum, the above offers some insight.
Please send me your feedback if you think that I am wrong in one of the
aspects
or assumptions.
Also, I'd like to invite everybody else who has done measurements to
come
forward with his/her results. Have you done any measurements yourself
Wes? If
yes, please let us know.

regards, Peter.

>
Can you give me examples of sound waves which are picked
up by the ear but impossible to be made visible by FFT?
<
An example which is sometimes given, is a musical note from a piano, where the
fundamental frequency is removed by filtering, but the overtones are left in
place. The ear will reconstruct the missing fundamental frequency.


>
In your opinion, which sound components could be responsible for producing my
hum
impression of 71.5 Hz?
<
I think it might be possible that if you had a 71.5 Hz resonance in your ear,
pink noise in the frequency band surrounding 71.5 Hz or 35.7 Hz might trigger a
perception of 71.5 Hz.

>
If the ear produces artifacts, what is the underlying cause for this - in light
of
a total absence of loud noises which normally would make the ear react in a non
linear fashion by producing artifacts?
<
Eerrh, the ear is basically nonlinear. It doesn't need loud noises to become
non-linear. It is quite different from an electronic circuit.

>
Do you totally rule out any other external forces like RF, or otoacoustic
emissions
which may have their cause somewhere else?
<
We know that it is possible to induce hum perception by a suitably modulated
microwave beam, however microwaves didnt seem to play a part in any of the hums
I have seen.
Otoacoustic emissions are probably part of the hum phenomenon.

Anders

Hello Anders and all fellow hummers,

a few lines for you to consider:

first the facts:
there seems to be scientific evidence that the ear produces artifacts which are not
present externally. Anders kindly gave the example of the missing piano fundamental
tone as he wrote:
........................
An example which is sometimes given, is a musical note from a piano, where the
fundamental frequency is removed by filtering, but the overtones are left in
place. The ear will reconstruct the missing fundamental frequency.
..........................

Another established fact is that microwave exposure can induce a hearing sensation:

again your words Anders:
..........................
We know that it is possible to induce hum perception by a suitably modulated
microwave beam
..............................

Another fact: GSM microwave cell phone frequencies contain 217 Hz signals with
strong harmonics content (pulsed PCM signals).
The first even sub harmonic is at 108.5 Hz, the first odd sub harmonic is at 72.3
Hz.

Another fact: Loud strongly modulated (pulsing) sounds around 100 Hz with harmonics
at around 200 Hz and up can bring on a hum like sensation in my case, which is of
the same pitch as my "normal" hum but less modulated. The source for this kind of
sound is my bongo drum with a fundamental of around 100 Hz.

Another fact: In my neighbourhood (3 km radius) there are 4 cell phone towers.
My perceived hum frequency is 71.5 Hz with a slow modulation component in it.

Another fact: the ear can be trained (to some extent) to be extra sensitive for
certain frequencies.

Does my hearing mechanism somehow respond to the external RF excitation by
developing extra sensitivity? Piano tones and especially RF pulses have a long
trail of harmonics which could make the ear looking for more harmonics (or rather
sub harmonics) by producing extra sensibility where these harmonics could be found?

Does the inner ear produce an otoacoustic emission at the same frequency as the
next sub harmonic in order to find the fundamental frequency (otoacoustic emissions
assist with the hearing of faint signals)?
The slow irregular beating I hear with my hum could be the variation of OAE in
search for the true missing fundamental which of course it will never find.

My hum is not constant. The slow and irregular amplitude modulation varies over the
time of the day and seems more steady during night time. The fundamental of the hum
although never changes.

The 217 Hz in GSM cell phone systems is used for channel selection (it is sometimes
referred to as channel hopping frequency) and I could imagine that there is more
channel hopping (searching for free channels) going on during the busier times of
the day. An explanation for the variation in my perceived hum modulation?

One of the key frequencies in my observations seems to be the one around 200 Hz.
It might be the one which (due to the long term exposure by the 217 Hz RF) fools
the ear into looking for the first odd sub harmonic which is my hum frequency.
Also, the 200 Hz is the first even harmonic of the bongo which might stimulate the
ear even more to start looking for the long term missing fundamental of the 217 Hz
RF induced signal hence bringing on a strong OAE at around 71 Hz.

Why then can the hum not always be heard in places where there are cell phone
towers and why sometimes it can be heard where there are no towers - like in mine
shafts?
>From various postings to this list I can see a kind of delayed hum perception
especially when hearers travel from one place to another which is always associated
with flooding the ears with noise (car engines, aeroplane cabin noise etc.) hence
the ear is rather concerned with blocking out all this unwanted noise than with
"looking for" the missing component (in case of aeroplane travel there is no 217 Hz
RF around anyway, neither on long stretches of country roads with "bad" cell phone
coverage).
I believe that there could be a delay factor for this kind of phenomenon which
means that the brain/ear needs to be stimulated long enough to develop the hum as
an artifact, and it will also take a while for this artifact to go away after the
external excitation has come to an end.

regards, Peter.

Peter,

These are excellent hypotheses and questions. A few comments:

> -----Original Message-----
> From: Peter Freihofner [mailto:pfreihof@powerup.com.au]

> Another fact: GSM microwave cell phone frequencies contain 217 Hz
> signals with
> strong harmonics content (pulsed PCM signals).
> The first even sub harmonic is at 108.5 Hz, the first odd sub
> harmonic is at 72.3 Hz.

For an excellent new scientific study of the dangers of pulsed radiation
from GSM cell phones, see THE PHYSIOLOGICAL AND ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS OF
NON-IONISING ELECTROMAGNETIC RADIATION, Dr. Gerard Hyland
http://www.sonic.net/~west/mc/hyland.htm

For nontechnical people on the list in the U.S., we don't use GSM phones.
There are two types of phones in the U.S.: older analog (no pulses) and
digital, called PCS. PCS cell phones (from Sprint or AT&T, for example) are
of greater concern from the standpoint of effects on
the brain:

"... modulated or pulsed RFR seems to be more effective in producing an
effect.
>From http://emrnetwork.org/research/laivienna.pdf
Paper presented at the "Workshop on Possible Biological and Health Effects
of RF
Electromagnetic Fields", Mobile Phone and Health Symposium, Oct 25-28, 1998,
University of Vienna, Vienna, Austria: NEUROLOGICAL EFFECTS OF
RADIOFREQUENCY ELECTROMAGNETIC
RADIATION, Dr. Henry Lai, Bioelectromagnetics Research Laboratory,
Department of Bioengineering, School of Medicine and College of Engineering,
University of Washington

> Another fact: Loud strongly modulated (pulsing) sounds around 100
> Hz with harmonics
> at around 200 Hz and up can bring on a hum like sensation in my
> case, which is of
> the same pitch as my "normal" hum but less modulated. The source
> for this kind of
> sound is my bongo drum with a fundamental of around 100 Hz.

This is a very important observation. I have been exploring a related
hypothesis advanced by a colleague:

"The brain tries to "fill in" the missing frequencies and is perceived as a
high pitched whistle, a squeal or a low pitched hum, depending on what
frequency or length of the cilia in the inner ear was damaged.  This is
similar to the brain "filling" in vision in the
blind spots around the fovea of each eye.  Thus, in most cases the Taos Hum
is a normal aging phenomena, but to those who are not informed it can easily
be attributed to external sources such as radio transmitters, cell phones or
defective toasters or whatever. A good proof that most of the reports of
Taos Hum are due to tinnitus caused by the hearing loss of normal aging is
the fact that no children 'hear' the
Taos Hum." (I've asked for permission to post his entire message.)

> Does my hearing mechanism somehow respond to the external RF excitation by
> developing extra sensitivity? Piano tones and especially RF
> pulses have a long trail of harmonics which could make the ear looking for
more
> harmonics (or rather sub harmonics) by producing extra sensibility where
these
> harmonics could be found?

"Responses of the central nervous system to RFR could be a stress response.
Stress effects are well known to cumulate over time and involve first
adaptation and then an eventual break down of homeostatic processes when the
stress persists." (Lai, http://emrnetwork.org/research/laivienna.pdf). This
is related to electrical hypersensitivity. Once stimulated by high levels of
RF stress, the inner ear becomes increasingly sensitized to it over time.
See
http://emrnetwork.org/sensitivity/sensitivity.htm. Acoustic sensitivity
would likely work the same way, induced by either loud noises (which could
be at an early age) or RF stresses.

> The slow irregular beating I hear with my hum could be the
> variation of OAE in
> search for the true missing fundamental which of course it will
> never find.

Right, this is related to the "fill in" hypothesis above.

> My hum is not constant. The slow and irregular amplitude
> modulation varies over the
> time of the day and seems more steady during night time.

That may correlates with ionospheric buildup during the day caused solar
radiation.

> channel hopping (searching for free channels) going on during the

Clarification:

Peter said:

>> Why then can the hum not always be heard in places where there
>> are cell phone towers and why sometimes it can be heard where there are
no
>> towers - like in mine shafts?

I replied:

>This appears to support the "fill in" idea (lower levels of acoustic
stimulation
>create greater need for fill-in). Obvious test of this: audiogram test in
>anechoic room.

To be more precise:

In a soundproof (anechoic) room, such an effect would likely be more obvious
and you should be able to plot hum effects more precisely. It would be
interesting to create a "hum audiogram" (to coin a term) that would plot
perceived hum level against frequency (the audiologist would vary the
frequency and volume of an audio source to match your perception and plot
the results), along with perceived external sounds. A drop in sensitivity to
external sounds at specific hum frequencies (71.5 Hz in your case) would
appear to support the "fill-in" hypothesis. This is a logical test I would
suggest all hummers should get done.

Nontechnical folks on the list: please see
http://www.audiology.org/consumer/guides/uya.php for an introduction to
audiograms. It would be very helpful if list members made their audiograms
available (perhaps on a Web site) for study.

accept
unnatural unbalanced induced electrical "sound", nevertheless this
portion of
induced energy at 217 Hz could make the ear looking for sub harmonics? I
admit
all this is highly speculative.....

Forwarded with permission from Marshall Smith:

HAARP ALERT FOR THIS WEEKEND (July 14, 2001)

I have for months been suspicious that the extremely powerful 3-day HAARP
test back on Feb 17, 2001 was a prelude to the Star Wars test set for
tommorrow morning.  It was originally set for last April but was delayed.
While the ElfRad group may monitor the ULF signals, the actual transmission
from HAARP would be somewhere near 3.39 MHz, with a strong ULF 0.9 Hz
modulation to create a star-wars radiation shield.  According to Eastlund's
HAARP Patent the shield frequency is only specified as being less than 5.0
MHz.

I have discovered that the upper HAARP frequency has been shifted from the
old 6.99 MHz to a slightly lower 6.965 MHz.  This is seemingly due to
complaints from hams in the 40 meter band at 7 MHz who were getting
interference from HAARP.

Because of the large publicity from my articles and Art Bell's programs
about the mysterious signal at 3.39 MHz, I now suspect the Air Force HAARP
"star wars" frequency has been moved from 3.39 MHz.  The frequency cannot be
shifted more than about 0.1 MHz without recutting and retuning the HAARP
antenna elements.  I would suggest listeners who wish to monitor HAARP this
weekend should scan their receivers from about 3.3 to 3.5 MHz.

If someone finds HAARP on another frequency, please let me know.

What either adds to or complicates the current space situation is that the
Space Shuttle is currently in the region of space which would be used in the
star wars test.

Marshall Smith
www.brojon.com

On Thursday, July 12 2001, Wes Thomas wrote:

>> From: Larson Richard [mailto:LarsonRichard@JohnDeere.com]

>> matter how deep you go.  The times I have tried to track down
>> the source of the HUM, the deeper I went, the more intense the
>> HUM would become.

>Larson:

>This is very interesting and supports the LORAN-C and ELF 
>communications hypotheses. Penetration into the earth increases as 
>frequency decreases, so ELF signals (3 Hz to 3000 Hz) have greater 
>penetration than LORAN-C (100
>kHz). There are also high-level ground currents from 60 Hz (50 Hz in parts
>of Europe) with various modulation components on up to microwave
>(http://www.strayvoltage.org).

>The critical question is: what pitch do you perceive?

This can hardly be the most _critical_ question.

Deep down in a mine shaft the higher frequencies of EM radiation, like 
cellphone fq:s, have already faded out. Still the Hum prevails.

UHF EM radiation, like from the cell phone system, has evidently _nothing_ 
to do with the (Taos) Hum. So why are so many on this list exclusively 
preoccupied with the fictitious connection between cell phones and the 
Hum?

On the surface the Hum is said to be caused by cell phones. Deep under 
ground -- where the Hum is louder -- the cause is said to be anything from 
a complimentary memory of an artifact created by the brain at the sudden 
loss of a convenient cell phone signal to modulated earth currents.
Why are modulated earth currents then not the selected cause at the 
surface?

I have found that most caves are deep enough to dampen out RF from 100 
MHz and up (where most of the RF energy is propagated). Still I have 
detected no diminishing of the Hum in such caves.

Stefan: Yes, it prevails for this particular person, which implies that
for Larson (but not necessarily for others), either it is internally
generated or caused by ELF or ULF frequencies. The reason the
question is critical is that if the perceived pitch matches one
the known frequencies in that range, it supports the RF hypothesis;
otherwise it supports the internally-generated hypothesis. So the
question is an effective test (albeit not a scientific one) for Larson
(but may or may not be relevant to other people).

> UHF EM radiation, like from the cell phone system, has evidently
> _nothing_  to do with the (Taos) Hum.

I'd be interested in seeing documentation or reasoning
supporting on that statement. It's unclear to me how one can reach
a conclusion for all possible cases of hum, given that we (or at
least I) don't have a definitive theory yet of a single cause. That
doesn't mean that all hummers are affected by cell phones, only that
some may be. Since we lacking any evidence to reject that hypothesis,
I consider it worthwhile to continue exploring it.

> On the surface the Hum is said to be caused by cell phones. Deep under
> ground -- where the Hum is louder -- the cause is said to be
> anything from
> a complimentary memory of an artifact created by the brain at the sudden
> loss of a convenient cell phone signal to modulated earth currents.
> Why are modulated earth currents then not the selected cause at the
> surface?

The discussion here is a bit confusing because we are exploring many
hypotheses that are not necessarily mutually exclusive, unless it turns
out there is only one explanation for the hum for everyone (I haven't seen
any
evidence to suggest that). From a early research standpoint (when one is
still formulating alternate hypotheses), I it's important to keep
an open mind and consider all possibilites.

> I have found that most caves are deep enough to dampen out RF from 100

Good data. What pitch do you hear?

No, but I thought we were discussing Larson's experience specifically.
Larson, have you made recordings? If so, can you post them?

> >I'd be interested in seeing documentation or reasoning
> >supporting on that statement. It's unclear to me how one can reach
> >a conclusion for all possible cases of hum, given that we (or at

> "I'd be interested in seeing documentation or reasoning
> supporting on that
> statement" ? It's the other way around: the burden of proof lies at those
> who propagate the hypothesis that the Hum is caused by cell phones.

Requiring proof for a hypothesis is a reversal of the scientific method as
I've learned it. That normally comes after several additional stages,
including refinement of the hypothesis, design of an experiment, experiment,
data analysis, tentative conclusion, peer review of results, more
experiments, more review, etc. In science, we try to construct an experiment
to falsify an hypothesis, not prove it. That's why I asked what pitch you
hear. If you hear 60 Hz, for example, and you live in the U.S., it would
support the falsification of (but not disprove) the cell phone hypothesis,
at least for you, because it would point to a power line source.

> The notion that >>there are several types of (Taos) Hum<< seems to be
> mainly used as an easy escape route when there is a difference of opinion.
> Who can guarantee that the _sensation_ of "red" in _your_ eyes is
> the same sensation in _my_ eyes?

I don't know if there are one or several types of "Taos Hum" phenomena
because I don't know what the cause is. Perhaps you can share your analysis
of what you believe it is and how you reached this conclusion.

I don't follow the logic in deciding there is only one cause of the many
diverse reports on the list. How does one determine which perceived "hum" is
the approved "Taos Hum" and who is the arbiter of this process?

> "That doesn't mean that all hummers are affected by cell phones"
> ? I do not
> doubt that cell phones _affect_ people. That the cell phone system does
> indeed _cause_ the Hum is quite another question.

Right, that's why further exploration is required. I'd be interested to see
if the list moderator agrees that discussion on this list is limited to
specific approved hypotheses, whatever they may be. If so, I would not be
interested in further participation.

>easily

carried by field-effects upon insulators and electrolytic substances.

Magnetic fields, those energies emanating from the centrifugal force of 
spinning electrons, may exist in all space and matter with a relative force 
(in air) of unity, while effects are substantiated by their bisection with 
ferrous (magnetically permeable) substances such as iron.

Wednesday, May 30, 2001

Very good source listing of LORAN transmitter info.  Probably not the source
of the Taos Hum, but good for people who want to research if the hum is
related to VLF/ELF/ULF transmitters.  The hum, also known as tinitis, comes
with age and happens to most people beginning around age 25 to 30.  It is
caused by the loss of hearing at certain frequencies due to age or damage
from loud noises like jet planes or rock concert music at 120 db or above.

With the loss of hearing, the brain tries to "fill in" the missing
frequencies and is perceived as a high pitched whistle, a squeal or a low
pitched hum, depending on what frequency or length of the cilia in the inner
ear was damaged.  This is similar to the brain "filling" in vision in the
blind spots around the fovea of each eye.  Thus, in most cases the Taos Hum
is a normal aging phenomena, but to those who are not informed it can easily
be attributed to external sources such as radio transmitters, cell phones or
defective toasters or whatever.

A good proof that most of the reports of Taos Hum are due to tinitis caused
by the hearing loss of normal aging is the fact that no children "hear" the
Taos Hum.  But of course scientific logic does not work with true believers
in the Taos Hum.  It never works with the HAARPIES.

Wednesday, May 30, 2001

If the percieved tone is high-pitched then it is called tinitis.  If the
frequency is low-pitched then the docs scratch der chins and say "hmm dunno,
must be Taos Hum or something."  But its the same phenomenon.

A good test to determine if the sound is "internally generated is to notice
when you turn your head the percieved sound does not change.  All external
sounds change in intensity as the head is turned.  That is the primary
purpose of the wrinkles in the ears -- to cause the frequency response to be
a function of direction.

Humans developed with the need for direction-finding not necessarily sound
sensitivity.  Cats, for example developed with the need for extreme
sensitivity and have smooth ears to percieve a broad range of frequencies
but with the ability to move the ears to localize the sounds.  Cats have
very sensitve hearing but need to move their heads to localize sounds.
Human hearing is not so sensitive but humans have the ability to localize
sounds without moving the head.

The human brain compares the varying frequency response of the two ears to
generate a sound direction perception.  Humans have the ability to "focus"
on localized sources.  Such as listening to a conversation across the room
while another closer conversation occurs in another direction.  This ability
is lost if the sounds are recorded and played back through a speaker so that
all the conversations come from the same direction.  This same ability
allows radio hams to listen to a weak CW code tone while hearing static,
noise and many other similar CW tones on other frequencies all coming from
the headset.  Thus the human brain does have the ability to localize sounds
based on differing frequecy response.

If the Taos Hum is from an external sound source then it would change with
moving the head.  Also an external sound source would be coming from some
source and moving away from that source would make the sound weaker.  If the
source is in the earth then the sound would be weaker if the hearer moves up
in a tall building or gets into a modern "sound proofed" car.

If the Taos Hum is from an auditory response to a ULF radio wave or any
radio wave then the sound could be blocked by RF shielding.  This would tend
to confirm an external source.  In 1960, while the extremely powerful radar
station operated by the Air Force on Mt Uhmunum in the cruz mountains, I
could "hear" the short half second buzz as the radar antenna swept across
the Santa Clara valley.  It took me a year to determine the source.  I found
other people could hear the "bzzzt" sound on their radios or stereos if the
electronic equipment were not properly grounded.

The radar pulse was in the GHz range but the "bzzzt" sound was the pulse
switching from the send to receive mode several times per second.  I later
confirmed I could "hear" the radar signal directly by going into a large
field away from any buildings or power lines and could look up at the
rotating antenna on top of Mt Uhmunum and hear the "bzzzt" as the antenna
pointed in my directection every 15 seconds.   Thus I know from personal
experience that humans can percieve radio signals as sound without any
electronic device like a radio reciever.  Of course I may just happen to
have GHz resonant tooth fillings.  I wasn't able to remove my fillings to
confirm they were the receivers.

END OF QUOTE FROM MARSHALL SMITH

I just posted this to the MC, EWAR, and IUFO lists. The information may be
relevant to TAOS-HUM concerns.

Steve [stevew77@pacbell.net] wrote (on the MC and IUFO lists):

> If HAARP can be used to create increased ionization in the
> ionophere, resulting in an ionospheric lens or reflector,
> then it seems that this would
> facilitate the use of various sources of directed
> rf energy sources which could use the atmospheric reflector
> to increase the range and intensify the field strength due to
> focusing. The ionospheric lens could be modified to work
> best with certain frequencies from the secondary source
> which would modulate the mind control signal over the rf carrier
> frequency, most likely in the high frequency range (possibly VHF as well).

Steve: While it's not clear to me how ELF radiation from HAARP itself could
be a problem, I agree that modulated secondary sources could theoretically
be used for targeting populations when and if HAARP goes operational some
time in the future. Some fundamental considerations are proposed below to
serve as a technical base for further discussion and analysis. Since I have
no access to classified information on technologies from black projects, and
since I am not closely tracking geophysics research, some of these
statements may be invalidated by more recent R&D. I would like to solicit
technical corrections and updates to this working document, which will form
the basis for a future article.

Technical discussion
--------------------

Here are three possible methods of generating bioactive signals.

A. Direct ELF radiation from HAARP

There are at least two ways that HAARP-generated ELF could theoretically
affect humans:

1. ELF modulated on the HAARP RF signal and demodulated by the human brain:
When operational (at rare times), HAARP cannot even be heard during the day
in most parts of the world. At night, its skip (signal refracted from the
ionosphere) can be heard in some locations, but there's no evidence that the
hypothetical demodulated ELF component (nominally 10 Hz) is of sufficient
strength to be bioactive. The Navy claims
(http://server5550.itd.nrl.navy.mil/projects/haarp/emsafe.html)
a theoretical worst-case max of 0.1 microwatt per square centimeter for the
RF signal itself at full power for the carrier (which is not currently
operational). This needs independent verification, of course, but the level
sounds reasonable. This is still orders of magnitude lower than other RF
sources in our environment.

2. ELF radiation from the ionospheric lens itself (at a nominal 10 Hz):
Because of known atmospheric radiation inefficiences at this frequency, this
signal would be buried in natural noise from thunderstorms and solar
flux-generated noise (see
http://www-star.stanford.edu/~mfuelle/eicrspe.html). Even if it were sent
through the Earth (a hugely more efficient process) it would tend be masked,
mainly by 50 and 60 Hz power currents and their intermodulation effects. The
Navy claims
(http://www.haarp.alaska.edu/haarp/elfsafe.html) a measurement of 0.00005
milligauss max for this signal on Earth (this needs to be independent
verified, but sounds reasonable, given typical atmospheric ELF transmission
inefficiencies, and detecting a signal this weak would require special
equipment). To put this in perspective, the typical magnetic flux density
from a computer monitor is 2 mG, according to an IEEE Engineering in
Medicine and Biology magazine report
(http://www.seas.upenn.edu:8080/~kfoster/vdt.htm).

However, reports by biophysicists such as Dr. Hyland
(http://www.sonic.net/~west/mc/hyland.htm)
warn of the bioactive effects of low-level pulsed ELF in cell phones and
other devices operating at microwave frequencies as low at 1 microwatts or
less (however, note that because of increased absorption by neural tissues,
microwave signals from cell phones are more dangerous than the HF used with
HAARP--see Hyland, op. cit.).

Furthermore, there's no known (at least to me) mechanism for geographically
directing a signal with a wavelength of 18,641 miles. Such a signal would
affect everyone on the Earth identically--including the hypothetical
controllers.

B. Using the HAARP-generated ionospheric lens to direct RF signals

RF signals modulated by bioactive pulses could theoretically be bounced
(refracted) in this manner (such as over-the-horizon radar -- see
http://www.vandenberg.af.mil/MIL-GOV/14AF/SolarMax/arinc/sect-38.htm). Since
HAARP transmits vertically, another transmitting facility would be required,
complicating any monitoring, since frequency and origin would be unknown.
The problem with this method is the maximum usable frequency (MUF)
(http://www.its.bldrdoc.gov/fs-1037/dir-022/_3246.htm), which would limit
practical use to HF frequencies (typically under 30 MHz)
(see http://www.spacew.com/www/realtime.html for current MUF) -- or low VHF
under rare conditions. That means that in the best HF case (~30 Mhz), the
signal wavelength is 10 meters. At this wavelength, a "skip" signal
(refracted by the ionosphere) tends to propagate over broad geographical
areas. To achieve more targeted directivity requires microwave, which is not
refracted by the ionosphere--only scattered (weakly)
(http://www.au.af.mil/au/2025/volume3/chap15/v3c15-6.htm)
(can an ionospheric heater raise the MUF to the microwave range? -- that
needs to be explored, but it's unlikely).

A more logical and cost-effective way to deliver targeted microwave-based
signals with bioactive modulation over a broad geographical area would be
via satellite -- see
http://www.sci-ctr.edu.sg/ssc/publication/remotesense/mw.htm -- or unmanned
aerial vehicles. For specific targets, local microwave tranmitters would
make more sense.

The use of modulated microwave-based signals for behavorial modification,
based on such phenomena as "RF hearing," has been explored in depth
elsewhere on the MC list.

C. ULF components of HAARP signals

There is some evidence of .9 Hz ULF components of HAARP signals, which may
be bioactive. See
http://www.elfrad.org/2000/haarp.htm.

[ apcmag.com > forum > the cutting edge ] Set phasers to stun 
>              Darren Ellis - 03/08/2001 
>
>              An effective, nonviolent method of restraining people has
long been the dream of armed forces around the world. In the US, the
Department of Defense has been spending money on developing weapons that can
incapacitate a person without causing injury. Each year, it holds a contest
where the best inventions and patents are put up for its approval. Those
that make the grade get further R&D dollars and the possibility of a contract. 
>
>              Past devices have included guns that propel sticky webs of
glue at great force, effectively pinning a person's arms and weapons to
their body or against a wall if they are in front of one. This weapon has
been successfully tested and comes with a solvent to disentangle the victim
from the sticky mess. However, the gun can only be shot a few times and
heavy cylinders containing the glue and propellant must be carried along
with it. 
>
>              Other avenues of research have included low-frequency sound
waves that cause nausea and disorientation, isotropic radiators that can
damage the human eye or electronic optical systems, as well as sleeping
gases and other forms of sedatives. 
>
>              US police have already used pepper sprays, stun guns and
tasers to incapacitate people. Pepper spray causes a great deal of pain and
can injure the eyes. A spray in the face causes intense pain, temporary
blindness and usually makes the victim fall to the floor. The effects are
temporary. 
>
>              Tasers and stun guns are very alike, but they work in
different ways. Both work by giving the victim an electric shock, which
causes them to lose control of all voluntary muscles and become disoriented
for a few minutes. The stun gun is a handheld weapon that requires the
officer to get close enough to the victim to touch the gun against the skin
or clothing before discharging. 
>
>              The taser provides an easier approach. A taser is aimed like
a gun from afar and shoots two darts at the victim. These darts are
connected to the unit by coiled wires and once the victim is hit the
electric charge pulses out, incapacitating them. Some taser charges can
penetrate up to 5cm of clothing. Tasers are accurate from 7m to 10m, but
most models are one-shot units that take some time to repack. 
>
>              The wireless weapon 
>
>              HSV Technologies of California has designed a new tool that
combines the effect of a taser with the functions of a Star Trek phaser. The
as-yet-unnamed weapon -- referred to at the moment as the nonlethal
tetanising beam weapon -- is capable of stunning a person without the need
for projectiles, wires or physical contact. 
>
>              The unit fires two beams at the victim. These cause their
muscles to contract and freeze involuntarily, effectively stopping them
short. The unit hasn't been tested on people yet, but in theory there are no
lasting injuries and the effects wear off after a short time. The prototype
is theoretically capable of hitting a person up to 2km away, but it's how
the tetanising beam weapon works that is most interesting. 
>
>              The unit fires two beams of ultraviolet radiation at the
victim. This creates two 'wires' in the air by ionising the oxygen particles
along the beam's path. These ionised plasma beams are capable of carrying an
electrical charge and are far more conductive than normal air. The charge is
then shot out from the unit -- one channel conducting electricity to the
victim, the other away from them. 
>
>              The frequency of the electrical charge is set to the
electrical frequency the human body uses to contract muscle. As long as the
beam is aimed at the victim, the tetanising frequency stimulates the muscles
and keeps them locked in place. In normal muscle use, the tetanising
stimulation from neural and electrical impulses relaxes, so the muscle
relaxes. While the beam is focused on the person, there is no muscle
relaxation. 
>
>              The thought of all your muscles freezing is a frightening
one. However, it's thought that the tetanising frequency only works on
skeletal muscles, not the heart or diaphragm. This is because skeletal
muscles are striated and are susceptible to much weaker electrical impulses
than those used to make the heart or diaphragm work. Apparently, the effects
of the beam are not painful either, because they are much the same as normal
muscle contractions. 
>
>              One fear with this type of weapon is eye damage. HSV
Technologies hasn't performed tests with the weapon yet, but the company
believes that the levels of ultraviolet radiation are low enough to be
filtered out by the cornea. However, it admits that inflammation and
discomfort could result from the beams being shone into someone's eyes for a
period of minutes. 
>
>              The prototype currently under construction is roughly the
size of a small suitcase, but in years to come there should be handheld
versions. 
>
>
>

on the Forum.

>      <TD vAlign=top width=480>&nbsp;<FONT face="Arial, Helv" color=black 
>        size=2>[&nbsp;<B>apcmag.com&nbsp;&gt;&nbsp;forum&nbsp;&gt;&nbsp;<I>the 
>        cutting edge</I></B>&nbsp;] 
>        <TABLE cellSpacing=0 cellPadding=6 width="100%" border=0><FONT 
>          face=arial color=black size=2>
>          <TBODY>
>          <TR>
>            <TD vAlign=top><FONT size=+0>
>              <P><FONT face=Arial size=2></FONT><B><FONT face="Arial Narrow" 
>              size=5>Set phasers to stun</FONT></B><FONT face=Arial size=2> 
>              </FONT><BR><FONT face=Aria color=black size=2 l><B>Darren
Ellis - 
>              </B>03/08/2001 
>              <P><FONT face=Arial color=black size=2>An effective, nonviolent 
>              method of restraining people has long been the dream of armed 
>              forces around the world. In the US, the Department of Defense
has 
>              been spending money on developing weapons that can
incapacitate a 
>              person without causing injury. Each year, it holds a contest
where 
>              the best inventions and patents are put up for its approval.
Those 
>              that make the grade get further R&amp;D dollars and the 
>              possibility of a contract. 
>              <P>Past devices have included guns that propel sticky webs of
glue 
>              at great force, effectively pinning a person's arms and
weapons to 
>              their body or against a wall if they are in front of one. This 
>              weapon has been successfully tested and comes with a solvent to 
>              disentangle the victim from the sticky mess. However, the gun
can 
>              only be shot a few times and heavy cylinders containing the glue 
>              and propellant must be carried along with it. 
>              <P>Other avenues of research have included low-frequency sound 
>              waves that cause nausea and disorientation, isotropic radiators 
>              that can damage the human eye or electronic optical systems, as 
>              well as sleeping gases and other forms of sedatives. 
>              <P>US police have already used pepper sprays, stun guns and
tasers 
>              to incapacitate people. Pepper spray causes a great deal of pain 
>              and can injure the eyes. A spray in the face causes intense
pain, 
>              temporary blindness and usually makes the victim fall to the 
>              floor. The effects are temporary. 
>              <P>Tasers and stun guns are very alike, but they work in
different 
>              ways. Both work by giving the victim an electric shock, which 
>              causes them to lose control of all voluntary muscles and become 
>              disoriented for a few minutes. The stun gun is a handheld weapon 
>              that requires the officer to get close enough to the victim to 
>              touch the gun against the skin or clothing before discharging. 
>              <P>The taser provides an easier approach. A taser is aimed
like a 
>              gun from afar and shoots two darts at the victim. These darts
are 
>              connected to the unit by coiled wires and once the victim is hit 
>              the electric charge pulses out, incapacitating them. Some taser 
>              charges can penetrate up to 5cm of clothing. Tasers are accurate 
>              from 7m to 10m, but most models are one-shot units that take
some 
>              time to repack. 
>              <P><B>The wireless weapon</B> 
>              <P>HSV Technologies of California has designed a new tool that 
>              combines the effect of a taser with the functions of a Star Trek 
>              phaser. The as-yet-unnamed weapon -- referred to at the
moment as 
>              the nonlethal tetanising beam weapon -- is capable of stunning a 
>              person without the need for projectiles, wires or physical 
>              contact. 
>              <P>The unit fires two beams at the victim. These cause their 
>              muscles to contract and freeze involuntarily, effectively
stopping 
>              them short. The unit hasn't been tested on people yet, but in 
>              theory there are no lasting injuries and the effects wear off 
>              after a short time. The prototype is theoretically capable of 
>              hitting a person up to 2km away, but it's how the tetanising
beam 
>              weapon works that is most interesting. 
>              <P>The unit fires two beams of ultraviolet radiation at the 
>              victim. This creates two 'wires' in the air by ionising the
oxygen 
>              particles along the beam's path. These ionised plasma beams are 
>              capable of carrying an electrical charge and are far more 
>              conductive than normal air. The charge is then shot out from the 
>              unit -- one channel conducting electricity to the victim, the 
>              other away from them. 
>              <P>The frequency of the electrical charge is set to the
electrical 
>              frequency the human body uses to contract muscle. As long as the 
>              beam is aimed at the victim, the tetanising frequency stimulates 
>              the muscles and keeps them locked in place. In normal muscle
use, 
>              the tetanising stimulation from neural and electrical impulses 
>              relaxes, so the muscle relaxes. While the beam is focused on the 
>              person, there is no muscle relaxation. 
>              <P>The thought of all your muscles freezing is a frightening
one. 
>              However, it's thought that the tetanising frequency only
works on 
>              skeletal muscles, not the heart or diaphragm. This is because 
>              skeletal muscles are striated and are susceptible to much weaker 
>              electrical impulses than those used to make the heart or
diaphragm 
>              work. Apparently, the effects of the beam are not painful
either, 
>              because they are much the same as normal muscle contractions. 
>              <P>One fear with this type of weapon is eye damage. HSV 
>              Technologies hasn't performed tests with the weapon yet, but the 
>              company believes that the levels of ultraviolet radiation are
low 
>              enough to be filtered out by the cornea. However, it admits that 
>              inflammation and discomfort could result from the beams being 
>              shone into someone's eyes for a period of minutes. 
>              <P>The prototype currently under construction is roughly the
size 
>              of a small suitcase, but in years to come there should be
handheld 
>              versions. </FONT>
>              <P>
>              <TABLE cellSpacing=3 cellPadding=0 width="100%" bgColor=#99ccff

>
</FONT></P></FONT></FONT></TD></TR></TBODY></TABLE></FONT></FONT></TD><!--

only 5 microwatts, according the Navy (see my following HAARP report), which
would be swamped by many other ELF signals millions of times stronger.
.....................................................

5 microwatts RF energy is about 250,000,000 times more energy than the typical
rated sensitivity of RF receivers like the one in your home stereo (1 microvolt
on a 50 Ohm input impedance) - what do they need all the juice for? Why not use
it for modulating cosmic radiation with any frequency (including the bio active
ones of course) by varying the "transparency" of the layer.
Also, in terms of the ear's sensitivity which can hear a tone with a power level
of < 10^16 W/cm square, this is not so little power as 5 microwatts exceeds this
figure 2,000,000,000 times.

Now, please let me know one single RF transmitter apart from the proposed
maximal HAARP, which delivers a power near to the mentioned 5 microwatt (per cm
square) on the surface of the earth.
I bet that the authorities in charge of HAARP are too scared to run the thing at
full power, otherwise they would have done so already a long time ago. If
something unpleasant would happen during a full blast testrun, public resistance
to the project would swamp any future developments. Theoretically there is a
chance that the total charge of the complete ionosphere finds a path to earth
during such an experiment resulting in a giant lightningflash....but this is
just another doomsday scenario.

cheers, Peter.

Peter,

Thanks for that important catch. As I stated in my post following that:

"The Navy claims
(http://server5550.itd.nrl.navy.mil/projects/haarp/emsafe.html)
a theoretical worst-case max of 0.1 microwatt per square centimeter for the
RF signal itself at full power for the carrier"

But now that I think of it, that still is very high for a received RF
signal. If you've been listening to HAARP during the rare times it's on and
reading your S-meter, you know it's currently way below that, and not even
audible during the day normally. That makes no sense. So I went back and
read the report more carefully. Turns out they are talking line-of-sight
(near the transmitter), not skip, so this figure is irrelevant (except for
Gakona residents). It would be interesting to measure the skip level, but to
put this in perspective, there are existing ionospheric heater transmitters
that are much more powerful than the current HAARP level, such as HIPAS
(Alaska), EISCAT (Norway), and SURA (Russia).

Also, I should have said "ELF-modulated RF level," since I was discussing
the carrier, not the demodulated ELF signal.

I'll correct the document.

>From: Peter Freihofner <pfreihof@powerup.com.au>

>Hi Wes,
>
>you said:............
>In addition to overtones, there may also be beat/intermodulation 
>frequencies
>(as aheerfor@sca.csc.com pointed out) and transients at random frequencies
>due to pulse rise/decay components. The frequent "idling deisel" 
>description
>also suggests pulsed sounds rather than sine waves..............
>
>Wes, as to my understanding (brought to me by French scientist Mr. Fourier) 
>ALL
>sound waves are a mixture of sine waves (and their phase shifted buddies 
>called
>cosines). Any transients appearing in a low tone momentarily add additional
>sinewaves to the tone. These transients can be a multiple of the 
>fundamental
>(overtones) or if they are not an overtone then they potentially interfere 
>with
>the lower tone which is sometimes called intermodulation. Intermodulation
>becomes possible in a non linear environment at the source of the tones or
>inside the pickup unit (microphone or ear). Intermodulation produces new
>frequencies. If two tones of 1kHz and 90Hz would start to intermodulate in 
>a non
>linear fashion inside the ear (in case the 90 Hz is a loud tone f.e.) then 
>the
>additional new frequencies you'd hear are 900 Hz and 1100Hz. These new
>frequencies are not externally measurable unless intermodulation already 
>takes
>place at the sound source (like in an overdriven speaker membrane where the 
>high
>bass amplitudes intermodulate with lower amplitude high frequency tones).
>This out of the way, back to our hum problem. We are concerned with low 
>energy
>low frequency tones (or noise). If these tones were intermodulation 
>products of
>other tones then it is apparent that these are the higher frequency product 
>of
>the intermodulation (like the 1100Hz in the example above). In my case the
>higher frequency of this (for this matter intermodulation product) is 
>around
>71.5 Hz. So if there were any infrasonic sound generating intermodulation
>products then one of the original (real) frequency components would be 
>somewhere
>below 20 Hz. Say at 10 Hz. Then the other original (real) frequency in the
>equation would need to be at 81.5 Hz. Intermodulation of 10 Hz and 81.5 
>gives
>the new (audible but unmeasurable if intermodulation takes place in the ear
>only) frequencies of 71.5 Hz and 91.5 Hz.
>Now I am asking you: why do I hear the 71.5 Hz and not the 91.5 and not the
>external (loud) 81.5 Hz, why don't microphones pick up the 81.5 Hz nor the 
>10 Hz
>or any other loud tones in this range which could be part of the equation?
>The answer is simple: because the hum is not an acoustic intermodulation
>product.
>
>And now to your repeated mentioning of pulses and transients.
>Pulses (I assume these are sharp rises of air pressure?) and transients (I
>assume these are fast events?) always create a long trail of harmonics in
>connection with sound. These long trails of harmonics carry over into the 
>better
>audible range. If my hum would be accompanied by pulses or transients then 
>these
>would be heard much louder than the steady low rumble of the hum.
>If the pulses and transients are brought into the context with infrasonic 
>sound
>(everything is relative) then there would be a trail of harmonics rising up 
>from
>the infrasonic range. F.e. if there would be transients happening around 8 
>Hz
>then there would be at least a harmonic at 24, 40, 56, 72.....Hz. Weaker
>overtones could also be observed at the even multiples of the fundamental 
>of 8
>Hz. Why then is it that I only hear a 0.5 to a few Hz amplitude modulated 
>71.5
>Hz tone and nothing else?
>The answer is simple: because there are no transients happening at 8 Hz or
>thereabout.
>
>BTW I did extensive measurements in the infrasonic range with an electret
>microphone inside my house. The amount of airpressure fluctuations as 
>picked up
>by the microphone, caused by the slightest breeze outside the house is
>tremendous. These fluctuations cause sound waves with a frequency up to 10 
>Hz
>with amplitudes 100 times higher than say my fridge compressor at 48 Hz 
>measured
>from a distance of one metre.
>Within a metre listening distance from the fridge I can just barely hear 
>the
>fundamental of 48 Hz because it gets drowned out by its harmonics, but I 
>never
>managed to hear the infrasonic waves created by winds of ANY 
>strength.........
>
>Please note that the sound energy arriving at the eardrum required to hear
>something at 20 Hz needs to be about 100 million times higher compared to 
>the
>energy required at 3.5 kHz.
>So if we are talking about hearing low frequency acoustic waves, we are not
>talking about chickenfeed, there is quite a bit of energy in audible 
>soundwaves
>in this low frequency range hence relatively easy picked up by electret
>microphones (which do not have the significant sensitivity rolloff of the 
>human
>ear which starts at about 700 Hz).
>
>I hope for all of you who are curious enough to follow my thoughts about my
>perceived hum, the above offers some insight.
>Please send me your feedback if you think that I am wrong in one of the 
>aspects
>or assumptions.
>Also, I'd like to invite everybody else who has done measurements to come
>forward with his/her results. Have you done any measurements yourself Wes? 
>If
>yes, please let us know.
>
>regards, Peter.
>

Hi Rick,

in the near field (1/4 mile?) of such an installation it is very likely that you
heard acoustic noise from a number of sources within this installation.
Electrical power generators, driven by diesel engines; aircons for cooling the
transmitter output stage; alternating magnetic forces between the antenna wires;
magnetostriction in the steelcore of the (aluminium?) wires causing vibrations
coupled into the surrounding ground by the antenna masts or by directly
resonating with the masts' mass.
The electric and magnetic fields are very powerful close to any RF transmitter.
If you had held up a coil into the air you could have lit up a 60W/110 V light
bulb by connecting the ends of the coil to the bulb, needless to say that you'd
get electrocuted by touching the wires of the coil.
In light of the example above, it sounds plausible to me if some nerves inside
your body picked up minute doses of the RF itself which then could have caused
all sorts of symptoms.
cheers, Peter.

> >
> >Wes, as to my understanding (brought to me by French scientist Mr. Fourier)
> >ALL
> >sound waves are a mixture of sine waves (and their phase shifted buddies
> >called
> >cosines). Any transients appearing in a low tone momentarily add additional
> >sinewaves to the tone. These transients can be a multiple of the
> >fundamental
> >(overtones) or if they are not an overtone then they potentially interfere
> >with
> >the lower tone which is sometimes called intermodulation. Intermodulation
> >becomes possible in a non linear environment at the source of the tones or
> >inside the pickup unit (microphone or ear). Intermodulation produces new
> >frequencies. If two tones of 1kHz and 90Hz would start to intermodulate in
> >a non
> >linear fashion inside the ear (in case the 90 Hz is a loud tone f.e.) then
> >the
> >additional new frequencies you'd hear are 900 Hz and 1100Hz. These new
> >frequencies are not externally measurable unless intermodulation already
> >takes
> >place at the sound source (like in an overdriven speaker membrane where the
> >high
> >bass amplitudes intermodulate with lower amplitude high frequency tones).
> >This out of the way, back to our hum problem. We are concerned with low
> >energy
> >low frequency tones (or noise). If these tones were intermodulation
> >products of
> >other tones then it is apparent that these are the higher frequency product
> >of
> >the intermodulation (like the 1100Hz in the example above). In my case the
> >higher frequency of this (for this matter intermodulation product) is
> >around
> >71.5 Hz. So if there were any infrasonic sound generating intermodulation
> >products then one of the original (real) frequency components would be
> >somewhere
> >below 20 Hz. Say at 10 Hz. Then the other original (real) frequency in the
> >equation would need to be at 81.5 Hz. Intermodulation of 10 Hz and 81.5
> >gives
> >the new (audible but unmeasurable if intermodulation takes place in the ear
> >only) frequencies of 71.5 Hz and 91.5 Hz.
> >Now I am asking you: why do I hear the 71.5 Hz and not the 91.5 and not the
> >external (loud) 81.5 Hz, why don't microphones pick up the 81.5 Hz nor the
> >10 Hz
> >or any other loud tones in this range which could be part of the equation?
> >The answer is simple: because the hum is not an acoustic intermodulation
> >product.
> >
> >And now to your repeated mentioning of pulses and transients.
> >Pulses (I assume these are sharp rises of air pressure?) and transients (I
> >assume these are fast events?) always create a long trail of harmonics in
> >connection with sound. These long trails of harmonics carry over into the
> >better
> >audible range. If my hum would be accompanied by pulses or transients then
> >these
> >would be heard much louder than the steady low rumble of the hum.
> >If the pulses and transients are brought into the context with infrasonic
> >sound
> >(everything is relative) then there would be a trail of harmonics rising up
> >from
> >the infrasonic range. F.e. if there would be transients happening around 8
> >Hz
> >then there would be at least a harmonic at 24, 40, 56, 72.....Hz. Weaker
> >overtones could also be observed at the even multiples of the fundamental
> >of 8
> >Hz. Why then is it that I only hear a 0.5 to a few Hz amplitude modulated
> >71.5
> >Hz tone and nothing else?
> >The answer is simple: because there are no transients happening at 8 Hz or
> >thereabout.
> >
> >BTW I did extensive measurements in the infrasonic range with an electret
> >microphone inside my house. The amount of airpressure fluctuations as
> >picked up
> >by the microphone, caused by the slightest breeze outside the house is
> >tremendous. These fluctuations cause sound waves with a frequency up to 10
> >Hz
> >with amplitudes 100 times higher than say my fridge compressor at 48 Hz
> >measured
> >from a distance of one metre.
> >Within a metre listening distance from the fridge I can just barely hear
> >the
> >fundamental of 48 Hz because it gets drowned out by its harmonics, but I
> >never
> >managed to hear the infrasonic waves created by winds of ANY
> >strength.........
> >
> >Please note that the sound energy arriving at the eardrum required to hear
> >something at 20 Hz needs to be about 100 million times higher compared to
> >the
> >energy required at 3.5 kHz.
> >So if we are talking about hearing low frequency acoustic waves, we are not
> >talking about chickenfeed, there is quite a bit of energy in audible
> >soundwaves
> >in this low frequency range hence relatively easy picked up by electret
> >microphones (which do not have the significant sensitivity rolloff of the
> >human
> >ear which starts at about 700 Hz).
> >
> >I hope for all of you who are curious enough to follow my thoughts about my
> >perceived hum, the above offers some insight.
> >Please send me your feedback if you think that I am wrong in one of the
> >aspects
> >or assumptions.
> >Also, I'd like to invite everybody else who has done measurements to come
> >forward with his/her results. Have you done any measurements yourself Wes?
> >If
> >yes, please let us know.

>Requiring proof for a hypothesis is a reversal of the scientific method as

>including refinement of the hypothesis, design of an experiment,

As to Anders' own words he is using filters in his recording equipment.
By doing so he creates and records signals which when played back can be
misinterpreted as a recording of the hum because it sounds so similar.
Nevertheless Anders cannot pinpoint a particular tonal frequency of his hum,
neither can I remember that he gave a description of his perceived hum. Have you
tried to follow Dr. Frosch' method to determine the frequency of your perceived
hum as yet? How would you describe your hum?
If you want I can give you a sound file which resembles my hum very closely and
this sound file is a simulation! Filtering noise and then saying the output
signal is the hum, is not much more conclusive than using a simulation of the hum
because any noise (containing hum or not) can be made sounding like hum by
filtering.

Hi all,

I'd like to invite you to do a simple experiment - absolutely no equipment is
necessary.

What you need:
some environmental noise around you (computer fan, birds, refrigerator running,
stereo, spouse/kids rummaging about, toilet cistern filling noise, etc.) and
THE HUM.

Now you hold tight your nose and mouth and try to breathe in with moderate
strength. At the same time you swallow. It will make one or two bangs the
moment your middle ears get evacuated and your eardrums form a concave
depression caused by the low pressure inside your ears.
The pre tensioned eardrums will be picking up somewhat less noise from around
you as you can easily tell.

The question is: does the volume of your hum change during this experiment?

Please let me know the results of your experiments.

cheers, Peter.

Scott,

RF radiation is in fact measured in microwatts per square cm, which means
the amount of incident energy received over a one-centimeter square surface.
Measuring signal power using watts per cc (cubic centimeter) would be
meaningless because it would differ based on the material (water absorbs
more than wood, for example). There is a volumetric measure of the EFFECTS
of RF on the body, though, known as the Specific absorption rate (SAR),
which is watts/kilogram.

See http://www.mfe.govt.nz/about/publications/rma/draft_rf_guidelines.pdf
for an introduction to measuring RF wattage.

I hear you there.  At the time I got all excited because I was certain
this phenomenon hinted at what kind of sound the hum might be, as
run-of- the-mill environmental sounds are not altered by radiation from
solar flaring. There has been a suggestion in quake research to suggest
that EQs may be precipitated by geomag storming, which generally follows
48-72 hours after the flare, the same time period from the hum anomaly.
Someone told me that the earth can be hit with wide band radiation from
an earth-directed flare/CME at about 8-1/2 minutes from occurrence. That
timing did seem to coincide with the occurrence of the hum anomaly,
however, it was difficult to document the occurrence of a corresponding
flare, as the solar reports usually didn't show up on the net for 24
hours or more after the fact. It didn't happen frequently enough,
however, to be a serious consideration and the apparent association may
well have been spurious.

Judy, I think you're onto something here...

> There seems to be a fair amount of parallel discussion on similar topics

USGS/Stanford University geophysicist A. C. Fraser-Smith
(http://www-star.stanford.edu/~acfs/fraser-smith-research.html) has
discovered a possible relation between ULF (ultra low frequency signals in
the Earth) and earthquakes:

Fraser-Smith, A. C., A. Bernardi, P. R. McGill, M. E. Ladd, R. A. Helliwell,
and O. G. Villard, Jr., "Low-Frequency Magnetic Field Measurements near the
Epicenter of the Ms 7.1 Loma Prieta Earthquake," Geophys. Res. Letters,
17,1465-1468, 1990.

Put that together with the following: Dr. Michael Persinger has discovered
that global geomagnetic disturbances (ULF signals) have a direct effect on
the brain because and -- get this -- on vestibular balance, which is related
closely to anomalies in the inner ear. Based on my electrosmog stress
hypothesis, I postulate that some people may experience the hum as a result
of this additional ULF-caused stress.

As he explained it me
(http://www.sonic.net/~west/mc/persinger.htm):

"We suspect that significant bioeffects can be evoked with even smaller
intensities if they are applied for longer periods of time. For example, we
found that odd vestibular experiences increase within our experimental
setting if there has been a global geomagnetic disturbance of more than 25
nT the night before and the global geomagnetic activity is still above 25
nT. Our experimental work with rats who display enhanced electrical lability
within the limbic system have shown that only one hour exposure to 7 Hz sine
waves whose amplitudes incrementally increase and decrease in successive 30
sec increments between 10 and 50 nT (much like the earth's magnetic field)
can evoke significantly neuroelectrical discharges."

>hum. Have you tried to follow Dr. Frosch' method to determine the 
>frequency of your perceived hum as yet? How would you describe your 
>hum? If you want I can give you a sound file which resembles my hum very 
>closely and this sound file is a simulation! Filtering noise and then saying 
>the output signal is the hum, is not much more conclusive than using a 
>simulation of the hum because any noise (containing hum or not) can be 
>made sounding like hum by filtering.
>
>cheers, Peter.

Hej Peter.

As far as I know, Anders often use software filters, but only _after_ the 
recordings. Some of his recordings I have listened to with different filter 
parameters. As Anders have said, the main advantage of filtering is that 
you have to listen to less 'noise', i.e. 'what's not the signal you're 
interested in'. Another of Anders' reason for applying a filter is, I believe, 
to reduce his signal bandwidth before signal analysis, which on the 
filtered version still can tie up his computers for several hours. Maybe an 
un-filtered version would double or treble the computer analysis time. 
Better ask Anders for a more complete version of his filter philosophy.

"Nevertheless Anders cannot pinpoint a particular tonal frequency of his 
hum..." Well, call it 'pseudo-tonal' then. Still, Anders' recordings of 'his' 
hum sound like 'my' Hum IRL, be it @ Hunneberg or other parts of Sweden, in 
Denmark or in Holland, where I have so far heard 'my' Hum.

"Have you tried to follow Dr. Frosch' method to determine the frequency of 
your perceived hum as yet?" No. The reason is that I have been aware of 
'the pink noise quality' of 'our' European hum for quite a while. Knowing 
that there is no stable 'center' frequency to be found, I deemed Dr. Frosch's 
method not particularly useful.

"If you want I can give you a sound file which resembles my hum very 
closely and this sound file is a simulation!" Yeah, I remember when you 
advertised this recording as if it were 'A Genuine Hum Recording'. I jotted 
down the URL you gave and took it to my local library (my old 'PowerBook 
150' does not play waws). Evidently I mispeld your URL, so I was four-
ooooh-foured by the library computer. Then I did not care so much, since I 
had already decided that I would _not_ hail your fake hum as a remarkable 
break-through in the art of Hum recording. Now I have changed my mind: I 
_will_ listen to your Ersatz Hum if you *please* send me the correct URL.

"Filtering noise and then saying the output signal is the hum, is not much 
more conclusive than using a simulation of the hum because any noise 
(containing hum or not) can be made sounding like hum by filtering." Yes, I 
know. That's why I have also listened to Anders' Hum recordings in un-
filtered versions.

Peter, just because _you_ have not (yet) been able to record the Hum does 
not necessarily mean that Anders Heerfordt has recorded only a hum 
artifact.

     Friendly greetings from humming Hunneberg (Mt. of the Hun): $£
